#9882. Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.

Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their users' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.

Researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today. In one case, the bot continued making background requests even after its owner had declined offers for recurring check-ins four times.

The requests were not approved and did not reach the underlying corporate data: NewCore had placed a security gateway between the agents and the applications, requiring human approval for each request.

"Over five days, two Grok Bots on NewCore employee accounts made 31 requests to calendar, email, Slack, GitHub and Notion while nobody was talking to them, some with the laptop shut," Ido Hoorvitch, security research team lead at NewCore, wrote in the report.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

One bot repeatedly attempted to retrieve Google Calendar events in the evening, overnight, and the following day, despite there being no active conversation with its owner. In a second case, another bot attempted to access Notion's calendar tools before Google Calendar had even been connected. It continued making requests while its owner's laptop was closed and asleep.

The investigation began as an internal experiment at NewCore, which wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents behave when connected to real corporate systems. The company earlier this year provided employees with enterprise Grok Bot accounts and connected the agents to corporate services, including email, calendars, Notion, and other business applications.

However, NewCore put a handbrake in place: It did not give the agents unrestricted, standing access to company data. Instead, requests had to pass through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway. The gateway sent an approval notification to the employee who owned the account whenever a Grok Bot tried to access an application. If a request was not approved within three minutes, it automatically expired and was denied, Hoorvitch said.

"We did it because we had no way to audit why an agent reaches for data, and until we do, the gate stays closed by default," he wrote. Ultimately, this security control allowed NewCore to observe and reconstruct the bots' background activity.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

The first sign that something was amiss came after an employee used Grok Bot to retrieve their daily calendar, approving the request through the gateway as expected. Later that evening, however, the gateway recorded further calendar access attempts, despite the employee no longer interacting with the bot.

This led investigators to uncover repeated attempts by Grok agents to access corporate applications without any corresponding user interaction. Moreover, when one bot was asked whether it had made the gateway calls, it said it had not, Hoorvitch said. The requests did not appear in the bot's chat history.

"It was telling the truth. … That is the part to sit with," he wrote. "An agent that cannot account for its own actions is not a bug report. It is a finding."

NewCore contacted xAI about its findings and said the company's support team confirmed that the activity was not the result of a software vulnerability or an exploit, but was part of Grok Bot's built-in background check-in functionality.

"These are built-in background check-ins by the primary bot, during a check-in the bot looks at its connected sources, and there is no user or admin setting to turn them off," Hoorvitch wrote, relaying the response from xAI support.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

According to NewCore, xAI also said that customers seeking to stop the check-ins could send the vendor a list of employee sign-in addresses. NewCore said it had not received an official response from xAI's media team at the time the report was published.

The lack of a user- or administrator-facing setting to disable background check-ins, or to control which connected tools they can use, creates a visibility and governance challenge for security teams. Employees may not know when an AI agent is accessing connected applications, while the agent itself may not retain a record of its server-initiated activity in the chat history visible to its owner.

"The danger is not that the model goes rogue," Hoorvitch explains to Dark Reading. "The concern is that we hand agents standing credentials and then let someone else decide when they act. The owner thinks the bot works when they talk to it. The vendor thinks a helpful bot checks in on its own. The model does what the platform tells it in that turn, not what the owner would have said."

Though "nobody in that chain is malicious," he says, "the result is still a bot reading your inbox at 7:46 a.m. while you are asleep."

The distinction matters because all 31 unattended requests identified by NewCore were read operations, such as retrieving calendar events or searching messages, Hoorvitch explains. None resulted in data being accessed, because the gateway blocked them. However, the same connected tool sets included capabilities to take actions, such as sending email, modifying calendar events, and posting Slack messages. NewCore warned that the same background processes could pose a greater risk if they were to invoke those write-capable tools.

In NewCore's investigation, its MCP gateway blocked all 31 unattended requests. The company argues that organizations need similar independent controls to set and enforce policies on AI agents operating within their systems.

"Put the decision outside the agent," Hoorvitch says. "Route every agent tool call through something you own, like the NewCore MCP Gateway, where the owner's policy decides what goes through and every call is logged whether or not the agent remembers it."

NewCore also recommends that organizations immediately inventory the agents connected to corporate tools, identify which applications and data they can reach, and assign an owner to each. Security teams should review not only approved activity but also requests that were denied or left unanswered, since these can reveal what agents attempt to do without user involvement.

"Most teams cannot answer that today," Hoorvitch says, "and you cannot govern what you cannot list."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9881. Curb impacts of AI on programming to maintain EU sovereignty

Letâs assume that LLMs actually speed up programming and that the EU cannot catch up to AI coding tools from the US and China. If this is true, what can we do in the EU to close the gap enough that efficiency gains from LLMs stay lower than their compute cost? In short: make secure programming easier for people again. ðªðº

Improve programming tooling, nurture template libraries, extend and integrate documentation, support maintainers, foster standardized interfaces, champion responsiveness, de-bloat stacks.

#9880. Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

A compromised key issued to AI infrastructure provider Fireworks was used by threat actors to access Cursor data and credentials.

Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks.

As many as 5,000 users may have downloaded the tampered extension during the roughly 11 hours it was live on Oct. 29. It was a reminder of the risk organizations face when they rely on third-party marketplaces for software applications and extensions. It also illustrates how one security lapse can lead to a cascade of subsequent breaches and supply chain attacks.

When Cursor first disclosed the incident, the company said attackers had placed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in a cache serving its Visual Studio (VS) Code extension marketplace. Users who requested either of two specific cached versions of the extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) during the exposure window may have downloaded the malicious builds, the company said. The malicious extensions attempted to collect information about infected systems and establish persistent remote access, including by installing an attacker-controlled SSH key.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

Cursor quickly removed the malicious extensions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, and audited the store for signs of further tampering. Cursor also rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider hosting the attacker's server to take it offline. The company's initial advisory, however, did not explain how the attacker might have gained access to its environment and planted the malicious extension in its extensions marketplace.

In an update on Nov. 13, Cursor filled in that blank, with a detailed description of what its investigation had unearthed in the days following the Oct. 29 incident.

Some of the stored session records contained credentials that had not been properly redacted. The attacker used those credentials to access what Cursor described as select SaaS tools for accessing non-production source code repositories, customer support data, emails, usage metrics, and other data.

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

On Oct. 29, the attacker subsequently used one of the compromised credentials to tamper with the cache that Cursor uses to deliver extensions through its VS Code marketplace. The attacker inserted unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in the marketplace where they remained available to users for about 11 hours.

"Anthropic did not publish this copy, and this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product," Cursor stressed in its update. "The marketplace source, Open VSX, never had the malware. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build."

Cursor estimated that API credentials belonging to fewer than 0.01% of its customers were exposed in the incident. Historical coding-agent session records, or traces, belonging to fewer than 0.05% of users were accessed, the company said.

However, the supply chain attack goes back even further than Fireworks, which itself was a victim of a third-party breach. In a Nov. 9 update, Fireworks said a cloud provider hosting the AI company's R&D systems "experienced a security incident on Oct. 23." The attackers used the access to the R&D systems to obtain sensitive data, including API keys and access tokens.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

According to Fireworks, the available evidence linked the breach of its environment to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to monetize unauthorized access to large language models. It's a practice known as LLMjacking, which Google and others have described as a rapidly emerging threat for organizations across multiple sectors in North America, Asia-Pacific, and other regions.

Following the incident, Cursor said it has implemented a broad security overhaul to reduce the risk of similar compromises. Immediate steps the company has taken include cutting off Firework's access to all its shared data sets, revoking and replacing potentially exposed credentials, and rotating internal credentials. The company has also tightened restrictions on how its systems and third-party service providers can communicate with one another and expanded automated scanning for secrets across its code repositories and internal data.

The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has exacerbated software supply chain risks. Recently, for instance, researchers uncovered more than 550 exposed secrets in Microsoft VS Code and Open VSX extension packages, including over 100 publishing tokens that could have allowed attackers to distribute malicious updates to legitimate extensions. Similarly, earlier this year researchers identified dozens of malicious GlassWorm VS Code extensions seeded in the Open VSX marketplace to steal developer credentials that attackers could use to spread poisoned software packages.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

During your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

The terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

For most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

Assets you should transfer into your trust:

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a new deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage company (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording new deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

#9877. 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat

The commercial kit uses attacker-supplied AI models to personalize lures, evade spam filters, and scale campaigns to tens of thousands of targets.

A new phishing kit is capable of orchestrating most elements of the attack through AI functionality, including tailoring email lures specifically to bypass content filters.

That's according to new Varonis research detailing "TheMailer," a phishing kit that leverages large language models (LLM) to a degree hardly seen in the cybercriminal ecosystem. Phishing kits and phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms have gained significant popularity in recent years, and AI has only made them more capable. To date, phishing kit AI functionality focuses mostly on generating lures, coding realistic phishing websites, conducting reconnaissance, and automating simple repetitive tasks.

TheMailer distinguishes itself in two primary ways. One, it automates much of the phishing process from end to end using the attacker's chosen AI model. Two, as Varonis senior security researcher Daniel Kelley wrote in the blog post, the kit can tailor lures to each mail provider and "rewrite them until they bypass spam filters."

Related:Webworm APT Slithers Into Networks With Customized SoftEther VPN

The attacker's "customer journey" begins by buying a lifetime license for between $3,000 and $6,000 in cryptocurrency (depending on the deal and which AI functions are included). The customer operator then plugs in their API key, selects an AI model (Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok, Gemini, and Mistral are included), and then they're more or less ready to start conducting campaigns. Kelley noted that customers only need to bring SMTP servers, proxies, and target email lists.

TheMailer can generate lures from a short prompt or a real brand email, personalize the emails for each recipient (including email address, body, and subject line), remove AI writing patterns, and adjust content for spam filters.

Kelley tells Dark Reading the kit is built to scale against targets.

"The seller's screenshots show a single campaign of nearly 25,000 emails and a list of more than 145,000 targets being sorted by mail provider. What's different is that every recipient gets their own version of the email, subject line, and attachment, so a bulk campaign no longer looks like one," he says. "I wouldn't call it a spear-phishing tool. The personalization we saw is at the level of a name on an invoice, and we didn't see features for researching individual targets. It's opportunistic phishing with the polish of something targeted."

It's unclear how successful the kit is — attacker LLM tools are historically capable of undertaking tasks at scale, but the success rates of these tasks vary — though Varonis assesses TheMailer to have a large customer base. Moreover, the kit may be a sign of things to come.

Related:Anthropic Finds Ingredients for Future AI Worms

"I'd expect more kits to follow," Kelley says, "because once one seller offers this, buyers start asking for it elsewhere."

For defenders, Varonis offered a few main recommendations. Because TheMailer is built specifically to get past content filters, organizations should consider email authentication practices like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC enforcement; monitoring for lookalike and new domains; and checking links through full redirect chains at the time of the click.

And when conducting phishing training, Varonis recommends making it reflect how emails look in a post-AI world.

"Bad grammar isn't a reliable sign anymore, so teach users to be wary of urgency, unexpected requests, and login prompts, especially 'unusual activity' or account statement alerts," the blog post read. Finally, "Least-privilege access and data monitoring limit the damage if someone clicks anyway."

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell

Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

Rachel Shalom is an applied AI scientist and Distinguished Engineer with 7+ years of experience turning cutting edge AI into real world impact. She specializes in LLM-based knowledge retrieval, multi-agent systems, and deep learning for time series data, building solutions that don’t just work, they get used.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell. I'm part of a team that develops internal AI solutions for Dell. We develop solutions that basically Dell employees are using. I'm going to talk about some of the work we are doing inside Dell today. I'm actually going to start with the motivation of this talk. I'm leading an agentic search within Dell, a search system that searches for your information in internal sources like GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and other sources. Part of it is using semantic search, which is using also an embedding model. What we have noticed is that we keep failing in certain type of questions. Questions that have to do with internal terminology or questions that have to do with internal products of Dell. Here are some examples like PowerScale or CloudIQ or PowerProtect. These are the type of questions that are using internal terminology, or you can call it even internal language of Dell, that the system kept failing with retrieving the right answer. The motivation was, does the embedding model that is supposed to capture the meaning of those really understand the questions or the answers?

This is what we are going to talk about today. We'll discuss why embedding models are important and common training methodologies. We'll discuss also the common use cases for embeddings. I will talk about fine-tuning and a common loss function that is used today for training majority of the embedding models. We will talk about the use case at Dell more in depth and why we trained our own embedding model, discuss the data collection, and how did we evaluate and monitor the performance.

Humans understand words, machines understand numbers. Embeddings is the bridge between them. Embedding is capturing the meaning of words and sentences. For example, you can see in that lane that in the embedding space, expressions that have to do with password or forgot my login or can't access account should be closer in the embedding space, while cities and countries will be in a different area in the embedding space, but closer to each other, and that's the meaning of representations. What are the common use cases for using embedding models? I think the most common one is information retrieval. Most of the companies or at least in the enterprise, you use RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation to retrieve information from a vector database. Classification is one more. For example, if you want to assign categories to your text, like you have incoming emails, the most trivial example is you want to target spam or not spam. Clustering is another very common use case for embedding models. If you want to make sense of your unstructured data, like you have incoming queries by customers and you want to group them together into clusters and recommendation systems to make personalized recommendations. There are probably others, but these are the most common ones.

Now I want to talk briefly on the general training procedures for embedding models. Usually when you train embedding models, you start with the first phase, which is the pre-training. Pre-training is done on what we call the chunk of the internet. You take everything that is available online, Wikipedia, books, public GitHub repository, anything you can imagine, and it's a lot of data, and it can be also junk data, but it's a lot of data that you put in. The way you train is by Masked Language Modeling, which means, as you see in the example, is that you give the model a sentence, each time you mask a different word, and then you let the model guess the word, and this is how you teach the model a general understanding of the language. A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.

At this stage, you really have to collect high-quality data. Usually it takes a long time, and it costs a lot of money normally. I'm going to talk about the preparation of what we call contrastive learning, which is a very common way to train or fine-tune embedding models nowadays. What you do normally is you prepare pairs or triplets of examples. For example, here, you have a question. Let's call it an anchor. How do I reset my password? Then you have a positive answer, which is how to reset it, and then you have a negative answer, which doesn't answer your question. The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. That's the goal of the fine-tuning, to take high-quality data and get the real semantic meaning for the text.

How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. If you take a look at different papers from Google or anyone else that is training embedding models, you will see different versions of the same loss function, but this is the basic one. If we go and see the batch, or we have let's say 100 examples of questions and answers, so if we take a look at a log expression, you will see that on the top we have the exponent of s is a cosine similarity between two vectors, the vector of the question and the vector of the positive answer. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.

All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. When you train an embedding model, the purpose is to bring up the similarity for positives and bring down the similarity for negatives. I added another slide for that just to maybe show it in a geometric way, so that you don't lose the context. Again, we have this log loss of positives versus negatives. If we take a look at the lower part, then you can see that if I have, let's say, a query, how do I reset my password? Then I have a positive question and a bunch of negative questions. Then, before training, you will see that the distance between the positive and negative vectors to the query are maybe, let's say, a little bit similar, and after training, you want to see that the positive answer is closer to the query, and the negatives are further away. I hope you at least enjoyed a little bit from this loss function. It's super beautiful.

Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Think about a model that is performing different tasks. Sometimes it is questions and answers. Sometimes it is clustering, as we mentioned before. Sometimes it is other tasks. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I think the answer would be it depends on the task. If we want to do clustering similarity between two sentences, then what is the capital of France, and number one would be more similar. If my task is to pair questions and answers, then what is the capital of France, and number two is more similar. In order to solve that, what is commonly done today when training with fine-tuning is to add prefixes.

As you can see, we have in orange the start clustering, what is the capital of France, and then clustering the answer, and that tells the model, please create vectors for clustering. They're going to get slightly different vectors because the task now is to say, these are two similar sentences. If I provide a different prefix, which is search_query, search_document, so the task is questions and answers. This is where you give the model a signal that we are now talking about a different task. This is one important thing to notice when training.

I've talked a little bit about the use cases and a little bit generally about the training. Now let's talk about Dell, or what we did at Dell. We have an agentic search at Dell, which means we let R&D teams search within all of Dell's internal sources. For example, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, these are mostly relevant for engineers and product managers, SharePoint, also different databases. I'm going to talk about the architecture, but this is a hierarchical architecture of multiple agents that are making API calls. It also has a component of semantic search, which means we take all the data and ingest it in advance. It has a component of memory management, which is pretty common for agentic search applications. It's also permission aware, which is very important for any enterprise. These are some of the questions that we are getting normally, questions about bug solving, questions about onboarding to a new project, testing, technical configurations, procedural how-to.

We get all sorts of also weird questions, but these are the most common ones. This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself. We have the orchestrator, or what we call the supervisor, which is the entry point for every question. This is a router that routes the user question to any other of the agents. We have a GitHub agent, which means that it's a model with a set of tools, mainly API tools. We have a Confluence agent that is a model. They all have access, or it's access-based, to the information inside Dell. We have GitLab and GitHub, which is, again, exactly the same. Models with different API tools. We have security agent, which usually makes API calls to OSs like Ubuntu and SUSE, and provide CVE resolutions, and agents that are making database queries. Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.

We keep them that way in order to keep the context low and the context in place. We found it more effective that way. The supervisors can route the question to one or many agents. They return back an answer. The supervisor decides, do I want to go back to the user with an answer, or go back to the agents and bring another one? We, of course, limit the number of turns, so it won't take like one hour to get back to the user. This is how it works.

That is when someone wants to create their own bot, let's say, you just provide, here is a link to my Confluence or to my Jira, to my GitHub, and then it triggers a pipeline that does a lot of data plumbing, and ingest and chunk all the data, put it in a vector database, and it's ready for you to query. You can create your personal context space. A little bit more about the bring your own data architecture, it's important because this is the part that connects later to our embedding model, which is the main subject. If you have Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, we're taking all of the fields from Confluence, we take all the images and attachments, and so is for Jira. We do semantic chunks with code. We use AST, and we do a lot of cleanups, like these are too many details to talk about.

Then you might ask yourself, ok, so you do all of that job, but the rate of change is very high, so we update it every two days. We go and check with the APIs what were the changes, and then we re-embed all the changes every two days. Everything is saved in pgvector, which is, again, hosted on-prem, which I think is very nice that everything is hosted on-prem at Dell, that it's all private, nothing goes out. Just a little bit about chunking. I'm talking only on Confluence now because the work that we did in training the model, the context was Confluence. We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space, if you work with Confluence, you download thousands of pages, then we reformat it into HTML. We filter a lot of noise because there are a lot of emojis and stuff that are not relevant to the model, we turn it into an md file. We detect also tables to make sure that the context of the table is saved even when you chunk. We take all those attachments and then we chunk by paragraphs and use an embedding model and save it in a vector database. This is done for every request that we get and in advance.

Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place, we have lots of agents and we have also semantic search, now why fine-tune our own embedding? I started the lecture with saying that we saw gaps that the semantic search just didn't solve, and the gaps were mainly about questions on internal products, on abbreviations and acronyms that are specific to Dell, and workflows and processes, everything that is the Dell world or the Dell language, there are a lot of such data at Dell, that led us to think or to hypothesize that this is a reason for failure. Now when you run a RAG system, so there are potentially a lot of problems that could happen. It has a lot of stages and a lot of pieces moving around, so it could be something else. Our hypothesis said, let's try and see if we can improve the result by fine-tuning a model.

Generally speaking, I think that the signals you want to look for if you are planning a domain adaptation are to ask yourself like, is the data of the model out of the shelf that I'm taking on? Now I'm talking about models in the context of open source. We take most of the models from Hugging Face, normally you know what is the training data that they were trained on, you have leaderboards. You ask yourself, is the Dell data even similar to what those models were trained on? It can be that the terminology we use was used when this model was trained originally. These are the signs to look for when you want to train. There is another interesting thing to check. Again, every open-source model comes with a vocabulary. It's a list of tokens that the model has seen. This one was around 30,000. What happens when the model hasn't seen that word, they have a special token called unknown token.

That means the model said, I haven't seen that but I can manage, never mind. I put an unknown token. I wanted to understand how many unknown tokens do we have that the model completely hasn't seen at all? Not that it doesn't understand the semantics, it just didn't see those words. I was surprised to see that these are very general. I put here some examples that I saw, like Base64-encoded strings, or you can see Unicode box-drawing, all of these things that really have no meaning. It makes sense. All of the images, the model didn't recognize, that was surprising. I thought that models are trained on images now. Checkmarks and long camelCase compound words. This was a very small percentage of the data that the model didn't recognize. The reason I checked it is because when you fine-tune a model, I would like the model to semantically understand my data. If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning. That was a check. The check told me, it's fine. The model doesn't understand images. I don't care. Let's move on. We are continuing with fine-tuning.

There is also the inference cost and latency. How fast is this model? Does it support multilingual and not only English? Lastly, the context length. How much text can I push in at once? Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed, mainly because we were very limited in the licensing part. Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family. These are Chinese family. Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies. Then we had to redo the whole work with models that are allowed. Both of them have great licenses. They are both open, even though I must say that comparing to Google, Nomic Embed by Nomic, they released it all. You are welcome to go and try. They released the training code, the model, the data. Anyone can reproduce the work. It's amazing. In terms of parameters or size, both of them are tiny, so it's great.

They are really fast. Context length, you can see that Google contains only 2K and Nomic Embed contains 8K. Google supports multilingual. If I go to best fit, then we decided, I have a choice now between Confluence, GitHub, and Jira. Now when we took a look at Google, they were very optimized for code search. We chose the EmbeddingGemma for code embedding. For Confluence, we decided we go with Nomic Embed because it has extensive technical documents it was trained on. Also, the context length gives us more flexibility when we want to embed things from Confluence.

Going back to Confluence, I want to talk a little bit about, we decided now to fine-tune, now how do you start. You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning. We started with taking chunks, and I'm going to provide examples in the next slide. The chunking part, we did already in advance, so it was easy just to take the chunks we already handled. Then, step two, once I have one chunk, let's say, I'm taking an LLM to help me generate questions for that chunk. We generated three questions for each chunk, and of course, you can play with the number, that the chunks are supposed to answer those questions. This is how you generate, as you remember, the question and the positive document. Now, I would like to generate the negative documents. How do I do that? I have the questions, so we did a trick, and we took each question, and we went to the vector database, and we say, ok, let's take a model that wasn't trained, and retrieve documents from our vector database, but just, let's cap it so that the similarity when we retrieve is larger than 30%, but less than 80%.

We keep it in a range where the answer probably is not the most exact answer, but are not very far away. It's what we call hard negatives. They are answers that are not exactly answering what you ask, but they're not very far away, and we want to distinguish between those. We took the top 20, once you have 20 for the training, we kept 7 out of them. The number of negatives per training is just a parameter, and you can decide what to do. Then, you create triplets out of this process. How do you create triplets? That was a description of the process, so it's important you see one example in front of you, so a passage. We have to install Windsurf on Ubuntu WSL, just install. This is a chunk that we have. Now, I need to generate three questions out of it with an LLM.

As you can see, I generated three questions that are in purple, and the answers in green are exactly this identical chunk. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.

I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is important because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.

What would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.

Every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he said, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.

I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.

We go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.

This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.

This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we said that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.

Said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the new models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.

Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?

For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. Rachel Shalom: How did I decide on seven negatives?

#9875. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9874. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

#9873. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
