#9872. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9871. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9870. Exception Best Practices

Good exception handling is difficult in any language, but all the more so in Haskell, where asynchronous exceptions mean that code can be interrupted at almost any point. In this blog post we will discuss a series of recommendations, focusing on three goals:

As we will see, satisfying all three of these goals together can be tricky, and sometimes they are in direct tension.

This is part one of our series on exceptions.

Part 1: Exception best practices (this blog post)

Part 2: âWhen an interruptible call isnât interruptibleâ, which will be published soon, discusses interruptible foreign calls: how they are meant to work, why they do not always work, and how to address that.

Part 3: â(Some) Exceptions in Haskell are resumableâ, also to be published soon, discusses asynchronous exceptions in pure code, resulting in resumable exceptions, and how we might generalize that to IO code.

Weâre also still planning two further parts: one on composing masking operations, and one exploring how the problems discussed in part 3 can be resolved.

In this first section we recap the most important concepts that we will need to understand before we can discuss best practices.

An exception is thrown with throwIO and caught with catch; in both cases the type of the value that is thrown must be an instance of the Exception class:

It is often more convenient to use handle, which is just catch with its arguments flipped:

Before throwIO can throw the exception, it must first wrap it in the SomeException envelope, which carries dynamic typing information and exception annotations:

This dynamic typing information is used by catch to ensure that only exceptions of the desired type are caught (that is, determined by the type of the exception handler).

Synchronous exceptions are exceptions that are raised as a direct consequence of executing the program itself. Haskell also supports asynchronous exceptions, which instead can occur at any point during execution1. Consider the following example:

It might seem that the handler should never run, but that is not necessarily the case:

If throwIO is the prototypical way to throw a synchronous exception, throwTo is its asynchronous sibling, and throws an exception to an arbitrary thread, although in practice it is rarely called directly; instead, it is a building block for other abstractions:

Without asynchronous exceptions, none of this would be possible in general: the code being cancelled would have to check, at regular intervals, whether it should stop.

Consider this code that attempts to read the first line of a file; it tries to make sure that the file handle is closed again if an exception is raised during reading:

The problem in this code is in between the lines; specifically, after the openFile and before the catch. The solution is to temporarily prevent asynchronous exceptions from being raised using mask, and only enable them again once we are safely in the scope of an exception handler:

The pattern in readFirstLineLOWLEVEL is so common in Haskell that it has its own combinator, called bracket; it takes three arguments, one to acquire a resource, one to release it again, and then the body that uses the resource. This means that the recommended, and idiomatic, way to write readFirstLine is

One downside of this idiom is that the exception handler no longer gets access to the exception. For example, if we wanted to log any exceptions that occurred while we were reading the file, along with the position in the file when the exception was thrown, we would not be able to do so with the standard bracket. It is of course always possible to drop back down to the low-level mask combinator, but in most cases it is probably better to instead use generalBracket from the exceptions package. When using generalBracket, the handler is told how the body terminated, and can also produce a result of its own (returned only on successful termination2).

(The reason for the fmap is that generalBracket allows the deallocation callback to return an additional value; here we just ignore it.)

Consider this version of readFirstLine that tries again when an exception happens; perhaps the file weâre trying to read might be locked by another process, and we just want to keep trying until we succeed:

Code like this with a blanket exception handler that catches all exceptions (by catching exceptions of type SomeException) is problematic. The obvious problem is that while some synchronous exceptions might be transient (âfile lockedâ), others might not (âinvalid pathâ); you probably donât want to retry on the latter. The less obvious problem is that you almost certainly donât want to retry on asynchronous exceptions at all: exceptions such as a Timeout or UserInterrupt (CTRL-C) should almost certainly be honoured.

Consider this variation of keepTrying; unlike in the previous section, weâre now specifically only re-trying if the file is locked, but we have a different error:

The problem with this version is that since the recursion happens inside of the exception handler, we might end up with an unbounded number of handlers, each next recursive call running under all of the exception handlers installed so far. In the previous section keepTryingBAD did get this aspect right: return a value that indicates whether or not we should retry, so that we can retry outside the scope of the exception handler.

Consider the following code, which spawns an auxiliary thread which catches all exceptions, and then shows that exception using anythingToString from my recover-rtti package, which bypasses any kind of Show instance (indeed, any type class instance at all) and shows the exact structure of the exception:

When we run this, we see (slightly cleaned up for readability, and some details omitted):

The outermost wrapper is SomeException, with the dynamic typing information (TrTyCon ..) and the (empty) list of exception annotations (ExceptionContext []), which we already mentioned above, and the innermost constructor ThreadKilled is the exception itself. However, we additionally have another wrapper in between: SomeAsyncException.

This wrapper serves as a marker for async exceptions. It is not an indication of how the exception was delivered (synchronously or asynchronously), and this is as it should be: the marker indicates intent (âthis exception was raised because of external circumstances, rather than the code itselfâ). Asynchronous exceptions are often caught and then rethrown synchronously (for example, see the section about bracket), which changes the delivery mechanism but not the intent.3

This does however mean that this intent must be stated explicitly. For example, in our first example of asynchronous exceptions we asynchronously threw MyException to another thread, without ever wrapping MyException in SomeAsyncException. If MyException was intended to be used asynchronously, we should use a custom Exception instance:4

Conversely, we can test if something is an async exception by checking for the wrapper:

In general, it is good practice to ensure that code that might wait for an unbounded amount of time, such as when acquiring a lock, can always be cancelled, for example through a timeout or through CTRL-C (UserInterrupt). Iâm intentionally using cancellability instead of âinterruptibilityâ, since the latter has a very specific technical meaning in Haskell, as we shall discuss now.

Note. Foreign calls in Haskell (safe or unsafe) are not cancellable. Alongside safe and unsafe there are also interruptible foreign calls, which we will discuss in part 2 of this blog post series on exceptions. The term interruptible, when applied to foreign calls, is related to, but not the same as, the âinterruptible operationsâ we discuss here.

When we discussed bracket, we glossed over one detail: it does not unmask exceptions when it invokes the acquire callback to acquire the resource, nor when it invokes the release callback to release it again. This is a thorny subject that we have written about before (Dealing with Asynchronous Exceptions during Resource Acquisition); here we highlight the two most important concepts only.

First, even with async exceptions masked, interruptible operations can still receive exceptions; paraphrasing the paper slightly: âAny operation which may need to wait indefinitely for a resource may receive asynchronous exceptions even within an enclosing mask, but only while the resource is unavailableâ. The canonical example is takeMVar, which can receive exceptions as long as it hasnât managed to take the MVar yet, making a pattern such as this safe:

will still be able to interrupt the takeMVar. Unfortunately, interruptibility is not visible from a functionâs type, and is typically not even documented; for example, putStrLn is interruptible (because deep down its bowels it calls takeMVar somewhere on the MVar buried inside a Handle), which means that this variation on withLock is broken:

The presence of putStrLn essentially pokes a hole in the careful masked state that bracket provides: if an asynchronous exception arrives after the takeMVar succeeds but before the putStrLn, the exception can be thrown (if there is contention for that handle MVar), and the putMVar will never run, leaving the lock forever unusable. A good intuition is to keep acquire and release as simple as possible; in the next few sections we will study some more involved cases.

When acquiring multiple resources, it is important that we either acquire all of them or none of them (atomicity). This means we need to worry about previously acquired resources when we get (synchronous or asynchronous) exceptions while acquiring more. The easiest option is to nest bracket:

Sometimes however the specific way that resources must be acquired and released does not allow for simple lexical scoping like this; or perhaps only offering a âwithâ (bracket) style API is too limiting at call sites. If you need to provide an API that acquires multiple resources, you have to think about how to deal with the presence of interruptible operations; for example, you might do something like

There is no point calling mask inside of takeMVars, because if the enclosing context does not have exceptions masked, then leaving the scope of that inner mask could result in an async exception being delivered at that point.

In general this can be quite tricky to get right, and it is often better to try and avoid solving this problem at all. For the case of MVar-like resources, the obvious alternative is to use TMVars instead, and just take both TMVars inside a single transaction.

If you must release multiple resources, you should ensure that if one resource fails to release cleanly and throws an exception, you still release the remainder; one option is to chain using finally:

In the standard bracket acquire release body pattern, if release fails with an exception, but it itself was invoked because of an exception in body, itâs debatable which exception should be propagated. For current GHC versions the exception from release is propagated, but starting with GHC 10.0, the choice is dissolved entirely: the exception from release will be propagated with a WhileHandling annotation of the original exception.

We will consider async exceptions during release a bit further down.

It is also possible to mask exceptions so that even interruptible operations can no longer receive exceptions by using uninterruptibleMask instead of mask:

This is safer in the sense that the takeMVar mb cannot throw an exception, but less safe because this code is now no longer cancellable: timeouts, user-interrupts (CTRL-C) etc. will not have any effect. To solve that youâd have to poll: explicitly check whether any async exceptions are waiting to be delivered, for example using unsafeUnmask (allowInterrupt, which does exactly this under mask, has no effect under uninterruptibleMask).

Another, possibly simpler, option to create an uninterruptible operation is to fork an auxiliary thread to do the resource acquisition. Since this thread is private, it is essentially immune to async exceptions.5 However, this will then still require some kind of communication protocol that allows the child thread to clean up when it realizes the parent is no longer interested; see also the discussion of Threads, below.

The ability to cancel code is often more important during resource acquisition than it is during release; acquiring a lock can take an unbounded amount of time, but releasing the lock does not. However, sometimes releasing a resource can take an unbounded amount of time also. Perhaps releasing the resource literally is acquiring a lock, perhaps to modify some kind of worker pool:

Or perhaps the resource is a connection to a server and disconnecting requires some kind of closing handshake to ensure an orderly closure (e.g.Â TLS uses closure alerts to avoid truncation attacks):

In this case, all the same considerations apply as during resource acquisition: the release callback is invoked with async exceptions masked, but interruptible operations can still receive exceptions.

In some cases you may want to vary what the resource release function does, depending on whether or not the body terminated with an exception, and depending on the nature of that exception (see also discussion of generalBracket). For example, you may (or may not) opt for an abortive closure of a TLS connection after a timeout; or you may (or may not) opt to close a file handle without flushing the buffer. Such decisions are of course highly application specific; a timeout may simply mean that the main action should be terminated, but the resource should still be closed cleanly!

Threads are a microcosm of the three goals that we set up at the start of this blog post: we must avoid leaking threads, communication between threads can get stuck, and exceptions thrown in threads often need to be dealt with outside of those threads.

New threads run with an exception handler that silently swallows the asynchronous ThreadKilled, as well as synchronous BlockedIndefinitelyOnMVar and BlockedIndefinitelyOnSTM, which we will revisit shortly. Any other exception is handled by the uncaught exception handler, which by default simply prints it (though this can be changed).

In general it is good practice to ensure no exception is ever uncaught.6 In almost all cases you should therefore install an exception handler in the new thread; what this handler should do will be application specific, but we will consider one important class of problems in the next section.

Consider a producer and consumer thread that communicate through a buffered interface such as an MVar:

The MVar provides back-pressure, which is good: the producer canât race ahead and produce an unbounded number of chunks if the consumer is not consuming them. However, if the producer aborts with an exception, the consumer will be left waiting for the next chunk which will never arrive.

There are a number of ways to deal with this. Probably my favourite is to record the exception in the buffer itself; this means that the consumer is forced to consider what to do when the producer fails:

Note that catching all exceptions here is correct: the consumer wants to know if the producer disappeared, even if that was because of an async exception.

Another option, arguably more compositional, is to use STM, and record the health of the producer separately from the consumer:

If you choose this route, it is important to read both variables in a single atomically block, to ensure that when the transaction is blocked waiting for a chunk, it will be retried either when a new chunk becomes available or when the health of the producer changes.

If you donât signal failure in the producer in any way to the consumer, the consumer may fail with a âblocked indefinitely on MVarâ or âblocked indefinitely on STMâ exception. You should regard this strictly as a debugging tool only, in the same category as Debug.Trace. Do not rely on it for your program logic: false negatives are common (where the exception is not raised even though code might be blocked indefinitely), and if you ever catch it, then false positives are possible (where code is not blocked indefinitely and yet the exception is raised).

New threads are spawned with forkIO, and inherit the masking state from their parent. We can take advantage of this fact to start a thread which starts with exceptions already masked.

Consider the producer thread example we saw earlier. A naive attempt to spawn a new producer might look like this:

If the producer is spawned in this manner, but is killed before it installs the exception handler, the consumer will be left waiting forever. For example, the caller of newProducerBROKEN is given the ThreadId, so it may kill the producer before the forked thread is ever scheduled. Masking asynchronous exceptions from within the thread cannot help here: the exception might arrive before we get a chance to call mask. Instead we must fork the thread with exceptions already masked, by masking them in the parent thread.

However, we cannot use the normal mask function; the restore function that it gives us will restore the masking state to what it was prior to the call to mask; we instead want to ensure that the new thread really runs with exceptions unmasked, independent of what the masking state in the parent was. Function forkIOWithUnmask gives us precisely this:

Note that there is a function in base that captures nearly this pattern: forkFinally. However, forkFinally does not use forkIOWithUnmask, but uses a regular mask, making it more sensitive to the masking state of the thread in which it is invoked; in particular, you almost certainly donât want to call forkFinally inside the acquire callback of bracket (see also Bracketing thread creation below).

To kill a thread, you use throwTo to throw a ThreadKilled to the target thread; this is such a common idiom, base provides killThread that does exactly this.

An important aspect of throwTo is that it is synchronous: it does not return until the exception has been raised in the target thread. This can be convenient; for example, consider a networking context in which we want to send a timeout message after a certain period:

The parent thread is guaranteed that the child thread wonât send the notification anymore after the killThread, without the need for any explicit synchronization with the child thread. It also has some downsides, however, as we shall see in the next section.

Threads are a resource like any other, and we should ensure that they get cleaned up. It is tempting to write

Both the acquire and the release of this example are wrong. First, as we saw above, when we fork a new thread it inherits the masking state from its parent. Since bracket runs the acquire callback with exceptions masked, this means that the new thread will now run with async exceptions masked at all times (modulo unsafeUnmask). However, even if we fix this by using forkIOWithUnmask instead, there is still a problem:

We saw above that throwTo is synchronous: it waits until the exception is delivered to the child thread, which means it must wait until the child thread can receive async exceptions. Because it might have to wait, it is interruptible; and unlike takeMVar, which is interruptible only if the MVar is not available, throwTo is always interruptible. This means that if this bracket itself is executed by a thread that is killed, we might not clean up the auxiliary thread. This is therefore an example of where the use of uninterruptibleMask_ is really justified:

This does mean that the parent thread (the one running this bracket) will be cancellable only if the child thread is too; an unjustified use of uninterruptibleMask_ in the child thread (the orderly closure example we discussed above), resulting in uncancellable child threads, propagates and results in uncancellable parent threads.

In this blog post we focused mostly on principles, not the larger ecosystem. We cannot possibly give an exhaustive overview here, but there are a few packages that we should briefly discuss. Two I can unreservedly recommend: exceptions and async. The third, safe-exceptions, takes an opinionated stance on async exceptions which you may or may not want to adopt; here we will only point out some aspects to be aware of.

The exceptions package provides polymorphic versions of the standard exception handling functions through a stack of type classes: MonadThrow for monads in which we can throw exceptions, MonadCatch in which we can catch them, and finally MonadMask in which we have bracket available. Itâs mostly a straight-forward generalization of the functions in base, with the exception of generalBracket, which we discussed already.

As we saw when we discussed threads, dealing correctly with threads is non-trivial, and async aims to make this better. It takes care of the following things:

Be aware, however, that cancelling a thread (implicitly through leaving the scope of withAsync, or explicitly through cancel), doesnât just kill the child thread, but waits for it to terminate. That can be important: if the parent and the child thread shared any resources, the parent can be sure that the child will not need them anymore. However, there are also cases where the parent does not need to, or perhaps even should not, wait for the child.

If you donât want to use withAsync, some of the old problems come back:

As mentioned, safe-exceptions takes an opinionated stance on async exceptions, which is provided through a series of alternative implementations of standard base functions: catch, bracket, throwTo and others all behave subtly differently in safe-exceptions than they do elsewhere. As such, if you choose to use this package, my strong recommendation is to import the package qualified, so that use sites (Safe.catch) are clearly distinguished from the standard functions.

The use of safe-exceptions should be a deliberate choice: it is not a drop-in replacement. Refactoring existing code to import from Control.Exception.Safe instead of Control.Exception, without making additional changes, is unlikely to be correct.

The first important difference is that Safe.catch and related functions do not allow you to catch async exceptions at all. This means that you donât have to worry about catching async exceptions in handlers that catch âallâ exceptions, though you probably should not do that anyway. If you do try to catch an async exception, the code will compile just fine, but the handler will never run.

In the section on distinguishing sync and async exceptions, we discussed that the difference is about intent, not delivery mechanism. We implied, though did not spell it out, that this intent is stated statically, through the Exception instance. However, in the implementation of throwTo in safe-exceptions this intent is stated dynamically: throwTo will add an AsyncExceptionWrapper around the exception being thrown if toException does not already add the SomeAsyncException wrapper. This gives a catcher the ability to still see that it was âintended to be asynchronousâ, but it also means that even if that catcher is defined using standard catch, and it has a handler for that exact exception, it wonât be able to catch it anymore because the type match will fail.7

The behaviour of Safe.bracket is also subtly different from standard bracket. The most important difference is that it wraps the release callback in uninterruptibleMask_. This means that the release callback does not need to worry about async exceptions, but as we saw in the section on async exceptions during release, this may not always be safer: in the network example, uninterruptibleMask_ around an orderly closure could mean that the code will wait indefinitely for the network peer to respond, and cannot be timed out or interrupted with CTRL-C.

The other difference in bracket is what happens when the release callback was called because of an exception in the body: depending on the exact nature of the two exceptions (sync or async), exceptions thrown by the release may be silently swallowed, making it all the more important to be careful if youâre releasing multiple resources.

Writing code that does the right thing even when things go wrong can be quite difficult; this is inherent, not accidental, complexity. Asynchronous exceptions make this significantly more difficult still, but of course also come with a lot of benefits; for example, without asynchronous exceptions a general combinator such as timeout would not be possible. Exceptions also tend to be non-deterministic, so leaked resources, stuck code, or unhandled failures may not be noticed during testing. Nonetheless, with some good code hygiene many problems can be avoided; hopefully the guidelines in this blog post can assist.

There are a few topics that we have not covered in this blog post:

Many thanks to Anduril for sponsoring this work.

The main reference here is Asynchronous Exceptions in Haskell by Marlow et al.â©ï¸

In addition to successful termination and abnormal termination with an exception, generalBracket also has a case for abnormal termination in monad stacks such as ExceptT. Since these are not strictly speaking exceptions, we will not discuss this any further in this blog post.â©ï¸

There are reasons to avoid synchronously rethrowing asynchronous exceptions; see GHC #2558, #24189 and #26368; however, those reasons are mostly orthogonal to our discussion here.â©ï¸

For the general mechanism at work here, see An Extensible Dynamically-Typed Hierarchy of Exceptions.â©ï¸

It would not be immune to async exceptions such as heap overflow, of course, but they are generally irrecoverable anyway. Strictly speaking it is not truly private either, as listThreads can be used to enumerate all threads.â©ï¸

The only technical exception to this is exitFailure, which should only be called from the main thread, and will throw an ExitCode exception.â©ï¸

Arguably, asynchronously throwing an exception with an Exception instance that does not use asyncExceptionToException and asyncExceptionFromException is a bug, but itâs probably a common one: simply deriving Exception is an easy mistake to make.â©ï¸

#9869. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9868. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9867. AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released new research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” said Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

When the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

The analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” said Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

The research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

#9866. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9865. Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

New agentic AI solution leverages APIs to collect compliance evidence from systems and applies it to over 30 frameworks with no duplicate work.

SEATTLE, November 18, 2026 — Strike Graph, the enterprise AI-native governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) management platform, today announced a new integration solution that seamlessly connects to any software API to automatically collect compliance evidence from it. With Integration AI, organizations using the Strike Graph platform are no longer limited to a fixed integration catalog. They simply indicate the system they are using and Strike Graph builds a native integration that pulls compliance evidence from it automatically.

Once connected via an API, the Strike Graph platform employs an AI research agent to read the vendor’s public API documentation and draft a build specification. Concurrently, a second AI agent builds the complete integration across Strike Graph’s backend, user interface, and evidence pipeline. Integrations connect API-to-API, and customers never install agents or software inside their own infrastructure, which is critical for maintaining enterprise-grade security.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

“For compliance to be successful, access to evidence must be quick, easy, and continuous, but integration with existing tools often presents a challenge,” said Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. “Integration AI has empowered Strike Graph to overcome those roadblocks and accomplish all three of those requirements at once. If it has an API, Strike Graph can collect evidence from it. Furthermore, since Strike Graph’s evidence model is graph-based, evidence from a newly built integration automatically counts toward every framework a customer pursues, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, with no duplicate work.”

As with all Strike Graph evidence collection integrations, Integration AI builds secure integrations that are restricted to read-only operations by default. Each one carries an endpoint allowlist that ratifies against the vendor’s real API documentation, which guarantees evidence collection can observe a customer’s systems but never change or impact them.

Strike Graph keeps strict separation where credentials are never touched by Integration AI.The build process works outside of the core governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) program itself, building the connection with no access to any customer secrets. Credentials and other sensitive data live in a securely managed secrets vault, and the build spec is scanned and automatically rejected if any credentials are detected in it.

With Integration AI, vendor documentation is treated strictly as data and never as instructions, which blocks prompt-injection attempts hidden in third-party content. The AI build environment holds no publishing rights, and a separate locked-down step does the publishing.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Builds sit behind an approver allowlist and a kill switch, and humans are always in the loop to review the research plan before build starts, after code has been written, and before anything is deployed to production. The AI can only propose changes, not ship them, and every integration requires a human engineering review.

Once built, Integration AI runs evidence scripts in self-contained isolated sandbox environments with no shared code paths, so a flaw in one integration can’t spread to another.

Integration AI is available to Strike Graph customers today. For more information, visit www.strikegraph.com.
