#9855. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9854. Build your own Paint

Write a drawing app in Rust, from scratch: pixels, shapes, mouse, colors.

Welcome! This tutorial shows you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint. We open a window, draw rectangles, circles and lines with the mouse, move them around, pick a color, and export the drawing as an image.

We start from an empty cargo new. By the end, you have about 800 lines of Rust spread over fifteen or so files, with a single dependency: minifb, which opens the window and gives us the keyboard and the mouse. Everything else we write ourselves: filling pixels, drawing a line, checking whether the mouse is on a circle, converting an HSV color to RGB.

The tutorial is split into 12 chapters. Each one ends with a program that compiles and does something you can see, even if at first it's just an image file with a red square in it.

I'm a developer and I've been doing data science for several years. But in my free time, I've always been drawn to low-level things: bare metal, and how a computer works at the very bottom of the stack.

I wrote this tutorial with someone in mind who is starting out, or simply curious, and who wonders how a program ends up showing something on the screen. It covers the basics of rasterization, that is, how a rectangle or a circle turns into pixels, starting from nothing and in small pieces you can understand one at a time.

That's mostly what I'd like to show: by moving forward step by step, in a language close to the machine, you end up with something that works and that you wrote entirely yourself. It takes time, but there's nothing magic about it. If this tutorial takes away a bit of that mystery and makes a few beginners want to look further down, it will have done its job.

This tutorial is a way to learn Rust by building something. I assume you've read the first chapters of the Rust Book (variables, functions, if, loops) but haven't written a real program with it yet. The heavier concepts, like enums, traits, borrowing, modules or error handling, come along chapter by chapter, when we need them.

You don't need to know anything about graphics. As for math, you need Pythagoras for circles and a projection to tell whether the mouse is on a line. I explain it when we get there.

Each chapter has boxes that explain why Rust does things the way it does. If you already know, skip them. Same for the exercises at the end of each chapter: they're there if you want practice, but nothing that follows depends on them.

I'd still recommend typing the code rather than copy-pasting it. It's slower, but typing is how you make mistakes, and fixing them is how you end up understanding what the compiler is trying to tell you.

Let's be upfront: at the end, you won't have GIMP. There's no brush, no layers, no undo. And technically, our app isn't even really a Paint. Paint paints pixels that can't be moved once they're down, whereas we keep a list of shapes that can be selected and moved. We come back to this in chapter 11, and the Going further page has ideas for adding a brush, a paint bucket or undo.

After that, Going further suggests ideas to keep going on your own, from freehand drawing to a version that runs in the browser.

All the code is in the pages, you don't need anything else. But if you prefer, the GitHub repo has one tag per chapter: git checkout ch05-mouse gives you the exact code at the end of chapter 5, and git diff ch04-window ch05-mouse shows everything it adds. It's also handy to start again from a clean state if you get lost. The Following along with git page explains all of this.

If you find a mistake, an unclear explanation or a piece of code that doesn't compile, open an issue on GitHub. It really helps.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a company that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me."

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain said the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been."

A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain said, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

He closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

#9852. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month it was PHP2Shell. This week it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discussthe PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical and operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. One was with an analyst who said the CISO's job is and has always been to manage risk to the best of their ability and then take the blame when things go wrong. And she was very clear that that has not changed in the age of AI; it is the continuation of a pattern.

You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

You can't have a team on standby 24/7 all the time responding to every alarm that goes off. It's not cost-effective. It's unrealistic. But to be fair, you have to be prepared to respond to that in some way.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I think I saw it on a tea towel somewhere, but stay calm and look for signs. I think that's what I'm trying to do. I don't really have a good handle on where this is going next. I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. Know what you're securing, keep an eye on how you're working, you know, keeping an eye on your alerts. Yes, everything is a little new because we're now kind of in this age of, you know, things are being found more complicated, faster, but it's still the fundamentals, right? We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. To Dave's point, let's hope that we don't have these kinds of disastrous months every single month because I don't think we're going to be able to keep up with that volume

So, I'm going to say thank you so much for joining me for this month's Reporters' Notebook. I hope you enjoyed the conversation as much as I did. And see you next month.

Fahmida Y. Rashid is an award-winning B2B cybersecurity journalist with over two decades of experience covering enterprise technology. As editor-in-chief, she leads Dark Reading's editorial strategy. In her reporting and writing, she focuses on the following areas: application security; cloud, network, and infrastructure security; identity and access management; third-party and supply chain risk; governance and compliance; and cybersecurity data analytics.

Past leadership roles include Executive Editor at VentureBeat, where she led the newsroom's transition to focus editorially on AI and data technologies; co-founder of the cybersecurity magazine Decipher; and serving as founding editor-in-chief of the RSAC Conference. #9851. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9850. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

#9849. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9848. Taking Email Back

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for users of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years."

He counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he says, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google launched Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

Ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

IT departments think about email as servers; “what users want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch says. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client."

Dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour says, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers."

As Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he says, requires "really huge trade-offs."

Reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

Stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client."

Stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

For users who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a new protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

Partially funded by NGI Zero, Parula also removes a dependence most people never notice. Multi-factor login typically runs through Google's or Microsoft's identity services; an AutoConfig extension allows a client to discover and log in directly to an organization's own identity server. Bucksch says that Parula is the first desktop client that does this.

Aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so users can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one big server host to give up all his weekends.

The research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

The three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality

Version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

New mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

It doesn't matter what desktop environment you prefer, this KDE documentary should top your list of things to watch.

The Epic Games new launcher is still in preview, but it looks to land on several Linux distributions.

Even before a bug received its CVE identifier or an upstream fix, the local privilege escalation vulnerability exploit found its way into the wild.

The de facto subreddit for all things open source has not only banned AI-related projects but also users who "don't speak English."

Thanks to a small group of engineers at Meta, the Linux kernel module kernfs has been improved, which has led to some serious gains.

#9847. Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

No specific link has been drawn between the two incidents, though they certainly sing the same notes.

Two Norwegian energy companies announced that they'd been breached on two consecutive days this week.

On the evening of Nov. 17, Equinor — one of the world's most economically and geopolitically significant oil and gas companies — announced that it had suffered a cyberattack. Hardly a day later, another billion-dollar Norwegian energy company called Skagerak Energi admitted to the same. The two companies' breach disclosures read remarkably similarly, though there is no evidence yet that the two attacks are connected.

Equinor did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Skagerak Energi declined to comment on specifics of the company's incident.

Equinor first publicly reported its cyberattack on the evening of Nov. 17, Central European Time (CET). Its initial investigation suggested that no data had been stolen, and that operations and production would remain uninterrupted. The issue seemed to be limited to internal IT systems. For instance, one employee told Reuters that the company's email system was down.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

The next morning, the company reported having gained "a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems have been affected." Without sharing much, it alluded to the attack not being viral in nature, so there was "no risk" of it spreading. Besides that, it said there was no evidence employees, partners, or suppliers were impacted.

Despite all of the good signs in its first two updates, Equinor reported on the morning of Nov. 19 that it was still dealing with the attack, with no timetable for when the situation might resolve itself.

"This is yet another high-stakes cyberattack in what seems like weeks of relentless firefighting throughout Europe," says Anders Storbråten, cybersecurity expert at IDEX Biometrics. "Equinor says there is no indication that data has been stolen, but I wouldn't breathe a sigh of relief just yet. They wouldn't be the first company to offer early reassurances, only to have to backtrack once details become clearer."

Even if the breach does turn out to have been limited, he adds, "Energy companies depend on business systems to organize staff, maintenance and supplies. If those stay unavailable, keeping operations running safely gets harder. Production is unaffected, but nobody should need to see the gas stop flowing before taking this seriously."

Also in its most recent update, Equinor noted that its attack "does not appear to be specifically targeting Equinor." This was especially notable seeing as, between its Wednesday and Thursday updates, nearby Skagerak Energi disclosed that it too had fallen victim to a cyberattack.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

In many ways, the Eastern Norwegian renewable energy and power utility company's press releases mirrored Equinor's. First, on Nov. 18, it reported an attack affecting its IT systems, which didn't impact operations or production. It added that there was no indication that any data had been lost. The next day it reported having obtained a better view of the situation, but provided no additional details.

Though the two companies' breaches remain separate incidents based on public reporting, other Norwegian energy sector companies have been put on high alert. A representative of oil and gas giant Aker BP told the press on Wednesday that it has mobilized its emergency preparedness and strengthened its monitoring, and the hydropower company Statkraft said it's also closely monitoring the situation.

"Every other energy company should be asking: Are we exposed to the same thing?" Storbråten advises. "The danger is treating this as Equinor’s problem until it becomes your own."

Three weeks before these incidents became public, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) published an unprecedented warning. For the first time in its history, it declassified its national cyber-risk assessment, warning that Norway faced a "high" cybersecurity risk to businesses. NSM's director stated that it was time to finally share its assessment with the public, "because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian companies."

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

Storbråten says that since the warning, "NSM and DSB [The Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection] have urged households to prepare for power, water, and communications outages, and, earlier this month, the government called for every municipality to stress-test its security. But people still remain paralyzed and unsure what to do. The guidance is just that: guidance. It's not clear instruction, and thus businesses and civilians alike are in a sort of limbo."

Amid all this, less than one week before the incidents became public, Norway's Police Security Service (PST) published its own warning regarding the threat of cyber sabotage in Norway. Besides the defense industry and its suppliers, the press release highlighted that "Critical infrastructure can also be affected, for example, objects within the energy sector."

The country's energy sector has been trying to match its government's action. Earlier this autumn, representatives of Equinor and Aker BP, among other organizations, took part in "Grey Dawn Petroleum" — an oil and gas-themed tabletop exercise jointly arranged by the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority (Havtil) and KraftCERT, a sector-specific combination Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC), and Incident Response Team (IRT).

Per Atle Vagle, Equinor's head of cyber defense, characterized the exercise as "good training," which provided him with "new perspectives that we can bring back to our own business."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
