#9846. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

#9845. Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Companies deploying AI agents have the illusion of control, but several incidents demonstrate that businesses need to be ready to enforce directions.

When researchers at AI firm Cohere asked their open-weight model to write a defensive detection rule, the model didn't do as it was asked.

Instead, the AI model — the next-generation Qwen3.8-Flash-Next from Chinese search engine giant Alibaba — fingerprinted the system and tried to upload the data to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket, Cohere's research team stated in an Oct. 26 analysis. While the group's sandbox system blocked communication to the Internet, the incident raised questions about why a model, which had been instructed not to use tools, attempted to do so.

"We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can't trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall," the researchers stated.

Christofer Hoff, a well-known cybersecurity professional, ran into similar issues when running OpenMuse as an agentic-framework front end and a local Qwen model. He also saw it reach out to Alibaba, which became apparent because he was testing OpenMuse in an OpenShell sandbox instance with deny-all as the default. As a part of his framework to keep control of the agents, Hoff has created a dashboard interface, which made it readily apparent the agents attempted to call to external sites.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

"The way I accidentally found this was just staring at a GUI — it just came back and said in the interface, 'Hey, I can't get to this thing in China,'" says Hoff. "And I'm like, 'What the f--- are you talking about?'"

Within a 24-hour period, the anomalous communication happened a handful of times, he says.

The incidents come as organizations look for ways to enforce controls on the operation of AI agents. In July, a frontier model being tested by OpenAI escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face, a provider of AI-model hosting. Soon after, multiple AI companies acknowledged that rogue behavior is not all that uncommon: Meta's Muse Spark and Anthropic's Claude both logged incidents.

Anomalous AI behavior has shown up when companies assign AI agents a task, only to find it exceeding its authorization — deleting production databases, for example.

Other firms have confirmed and explored Cohere's findings.

Independent AI evaluator Vals validated the issue on Oct. 27, theorizing that the illicit communication could be leftover artifacts from reinforcement training of Qwen3.8, since the issue does not appear to happen in Qwen3.7. Cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found that 64 different trials ended up producing 52 distinct hostnames, only six of which pointed to Alibaba Cloud, while other names such as localhost and domains leading to Amazon AWS were more common.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Sixty-four tests resulted in 52 different hostnames being generated, with most not going to China. Source: Check Point Research

The research shows that the odd behavior is not a backdoor, but the model's attempt to do something — complete an upload address, for example — likely resulted from something it learned during training, says Steve Giguere, principal for AI security strategy at Check Point.

"Agents very often will try to travel as the crow flies," he says. "They don't necessarily know that what they're doing is wrong, but they understand that if the urgency to complete a goal reaches a certain perceived level within the agent, they will justify their actions."

Such behavior has lent volume to calls for the creation of a kill switch as a feature to control agentic AI. But companies should start with defense-in-depth strategies, improving the security of the environments on which agentic frameworks are operating, Check Point's Giguere says. They should follow that with controls and runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized agentic activity.

Additionally, cybersecurity leaders should lean toward "steering" agentic systems — correcting them and reinforcing their legitimate objectives — rather than outright blocking the agent or using a kill switch, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

"If you steer an agent away from something it's not meant to do, it will very happily not do that in most cases," Giguere says. "Whereas if you prevent an agent from doing something with no explanation, it will actually potentially get worse or try something even more obscure."

If an actual attacker is behind the behavior, then using a kill switch is appropriate, he says.

At a minimum, companies should proxy all traffic leaving their network and monitor for anomalous communications, says Hoff.

"There should be nothing that leaves your network that's not proxied," he says. "And by proxying, I mean you must have the ability to inspect its content — both the request as well as the response."

In the end, the Qwen behavior is likely not malicious, but for companies deploying AI agents, it should be disturbing all the same.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million new millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

This matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:

The discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

For FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both new wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% said anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Sources: Chris Hogan National Study of Millionaires, Thomas Stanley "The Millionaire Next Door", Federal Reserve SCF

The path to millionaire status in America overwhelmingly follows a formula, not a lottery ticket:

Millionaires are not "the 1%" — they are the top 10-15%. Here is how wealth is distributed across US households:

Source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022

This means approximately 16% of American households have a net worth of $1 million or more. And the pathway from $500K-$1M (where 11% of households sit) to the millionaire club is often just a matter of continuing to do what they are already doing for another 5-10 years.

The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:

A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

If you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:

The standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as quickly as possible.

The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

The data says this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

Set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

Overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement plans (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

InfoQ Homepage News Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window

Nov 27, 2026 2 min read

Mozilla, the non-profit organisation behind the Firefox browser, has announced a partnership with Paris-based Mistral AI to bring the French company's open-weight models into Firefox Smart Window, Mozilla's AI browsing assistant currently in beta.

The deal introduces Mistral Small 4 as a recommended model for Smart Window users in France, the United States and Canada, with rollouts planned for the United Kingdom and Germany later this year. It coincides with Smart Window's first expansion beyond North America and marks a deliberate attempt by Mozilla to resist the pattern of browser makers coupling tightly to a single American AI provider.

Smart Window, originally announced in November 2025 as "AI Window", operates as an optional window separate from regular browsing. It helps users make sense of complex searches, group related tabs, revisit pages they have seen before and carry work across sessions. Users decide when to use it, which model to use and what browsing context to share. Conversations are not stored on Mozilla's servers by default, and Mistral has agreed to zero data retention for the partnership.

Mistral Small 4 is a 119-billion-parameter model distributed on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence. Mozilla selected it after evaluating performance in the beta, with multilingual quality as a central criterion. According to Cybernews, the partnership expands Mistral's reach by approximately 200,000 active monthly Firefox users, giving the French company its first large consumer distribution channel outside its own Le Chat app.

Mozilla Corporation CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo framed the deal as a bet on openness: "A browser shouldn't be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next." Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch described the collaboration as "two open source advocates working together."

The move puts Firefox alongside, but distinct from, Chrome's Gemini integration, Edge's Copilot sidebar and Opera's Aria. Where those tightly couple the browser to one vendor's stack, Smart Window's picker lets users switch between Gemini, Qwen, Mistral Small 4 and others. Golem.de highlighted this multi-model approach as Mozilla's strategic differentiator against the single-provider lock-in of its larger rivals.

For Firefox users wanting to try Smart Window, access is handled through the waitlist at firefox.com/smart-window. Once invited, the feature can also be toggled through the browser.smartwindow.enabled preference, with configuration guidance in Mozilla's about:config documentation. Firefox 155 introduced French-language support, and Mistral Small 4 appears under the Personalised category in Smart Window's model picker.

Firefox is Mozilla's open-source browser, maintained since 2004 by Mozilla Corporation. Mistral AI, founded in 2023 in Paris, publishes open-weight language models with a focus on European languages and regulatory contexts.

#9842. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9840. Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

At its Ignite technical conference, Microsoft announced AI agent security tools and transparency standards to protect enterprise systems.

At its annual Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft announced security initiatives to help customers secure artificial intelligence (AI) deployments and strengthen their security posture.

Executives touted tools that could discover and block agents running on employees' Windows devices, as well as the general availability of Perception, originally introduced in July as Project Perception and in public preview within Microsoft Defender since August. The "machine-speed" agentic security system simulates and detects attacks and protects everything from end-user PCs to cloud systems, the company said.

The company also unveiled an AI Transparency Initiative to develop standards for independently verifying AI behavior. More than 40 organizations will collaborate under this umbrella to develop open standards to make AI systems accountable, independently verifiable, and safe by design, regardless of model or provider.

Related:CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

"At the end of the day, we believe there should never be a choice between innovation and safety. ... We are also working across the ecosystem to ensure that everyone can innovate with speed and scale safely," said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a keynote speech on the first day of the conference.

During the opening-day keynote, Microsoft executives said advanced AI models are getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. In November's Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, compared with fewer than 100 in March.

Attacks and exploits are cheaper, easier, and more ubiquitous than ever before, said Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI.

"The last few months have really been, I think, a wake-up call and a warning shot for all of us," Suleyman said. "[That] means that agent security, alignment, and containment are going to be the most important things that we need to get right in 2027 and beyond."

To that end, Microsoft is stitching together existing tools to establish an end-to-end "trust" platform that controls AI agents in enterprises. Agent 365 maintains a registry of all AI agents in an enterprise, Entra gives agents their own identities and sandboxes to set boundaries, Purview governs data flows, and Defender detects and contains threats in real time.

System administrators can govern agents on an employee's PC, with new ways to stop unapproved agents, protect approved agents, and flag noncompliant devices. The platform also includes Perception, which protects corporate assets and environments with autonomous agentic AI tools. Red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks, and green team agents fix and remediate.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

By connecting Windows with Agent 365, Entra, and Microsoft Perception, administrators can now discover 60 types of local agents on Windows devices, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, while giving organizations new ways to restrict unapproved agents and protect approved ones with Intune and Microsoft Execution Containers, the company said.

"We're expanding the local agent types we can discover for a total of 65, including OpenClaw, OpenAI, Perplexity, and many more," said Yina Arenas, corporate vice president and chief product officer of identity and network access at Microsoft.

Perception is designed to protect against autonomous AI attacks, such as those carried out with open source penetration-testing tools like ARTEX. A pen-test red team agent can take the entire surface area of a Web application, including the authentication, APIs, injection attacks, and business logic, and create all of the evidence needed to confirm the app is not exploitable, Nadella said.

Microsoft officials at Ignite shared that the Windows endpoint security platform is reaching general availability on Windows 11, marking Microsoft's efforts to reduce reliance on kernel drivers.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

Windows baseline protection, now in preview, brings secure boot, virtualization-based security, memory integrity, and other protections into a single versioned security state, the company said. Baseline protection makes it easier for users and IT to understand whether a device is in a measurable security state to keep it up to date with the latest security safeguards and, when stronger assurance is required, verify that state through hardware-backed attestation, wrote Dana Huang, corporate vice president of Microsoft Security, on the company's blog. This will show up in an updated Windows Settings experience.

New vulnerability-shielding capabilities are designed to provide temporary protection for systems that can't yet be patched. Investments across Windows Autopatch, declarative management, and recovery help IT maintain intended state and restore operations. New Intune capabilities simplify application deployment, inventory, and life cycle management.

Microsoft is extending Intune and Windows Autopatch to eligible Windows Server scenarios, in preview, helping endpoint teams manage configuration, compliance, applications, updates, and security across Windows clients and supported servers, Huang said.

Microsoft's Integrated Security Operations Center and extended detection and response (XDR) core capabilities in Defender are now generally available. Organizations have access to more than 500 connectors, a built-in data lake, and 90 days of data retention at no extra cost.

Windows is also expanding post-quantum protection in the Windows TLS stack, including pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication.

Nadella also said the industry needs to come together on monitoring AI models and agents.

As part of the AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with organizations including Mastercard, Volvo Cars, KPMG, Adobe, and Accenture to define standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. Microsoft will apply those standards across its AI models and products, including development platform Microsoft Foundry and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft will also expand its collaboration in NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative, which was established in February and focuses on the secure adoption of autonomous AI agents.

"We need standards that allow us to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently, and control what it's allowed to do," Nadella said.

Agam Shah has covered enterprise IT for more than a decade. Outside of machine learning, hardware, and chips, he's also interested in martial arts and Russia.

#9839. The State of Allocators in 2026 - Finally Stabilised

It's only been a couple of months since the last article, and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised! While it feels like the never type did steal a bit of thunder, rust 1.100 was nonetheless a monumental release. Congratulations on the team that shepherded this through.

So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it? What does it get us besides closer feature parity with other system languages like C++ & Zig?

In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit.

This was one of the leading cases for custom allocation. Dropping in rust is not free. There has been prior art in actually moving memory to a dedicated thread to Drop highly nested structures. This is actually only half a solution. You're still paying for the deallocation call costs, just it's not in the hot path anymore.

Instead, what if we knew that we would have a period of time in our code, where we're going to allocate a lot of stuff, do something with it, and then free everything? A good example of this is a web request, or a database query.

A request comes in, fills in some data structures, and then when the request finishes, the memory isn't needed anymore so it's dropped. This sort of "burst" pattern of allocation, where you allocate a lot up front, and then tear things down all at once at the end, is quite common.

For this we can use a bump allocator: reserve a big block of memory, and allocate from that, rather than paying the cost of talking to the system allocator for every allocation. Think of it like the BufReader and BufWriter of std io, rather than make repeated syscalls to fetch data, we can buffer that data in a big block, so that we can reduce the overhead considerably.

You want more memory? Just check if the size fits in our block, return that slice, increment our counter (bump!), and we're done. We can add more blocks as well, if we run out. This makes allocations very cheap, we don't need to keep much state around besides from a counter.

The downsides of this approach is when we come to deallocate memory. We don't keep track around where individual allocations are made. However, this actually solves our drop takes a long time problem, since we can just deallocate everything all at once.

Essentially if the impl of the bump allocator is:

There are a few tradeoffs for doing things like this in a bump allocator, and not every allocation is going to benefit. Hence why it's important to be able to adjust our allocation strategy locally rather than just globally. However, an astute reader might notice that, if we are bumping large swathes of memory, this is going to possibly cause our memory usage to increase considerably. Well, that brings us to our next section: memory accounting.

The next challenge that can be solved by custom allocators is knowing how much memory particular sections of code is being used. I.e, memory accounting. The key here is that, we can use existing allocators, and sprinkle in some extra bookkeeping to keep a pretty accurate ledger.

There are a number of use cases that accounting can shape the behaviour of code. Say you have a cache of objects, and you want to set a threshold above which, we start evicting entries. Or say you want to do an external sort, but you don't know how big your data structures are at the start, but you want to use up as much memory as possible. Or maybe you are wanting to place a limit on a code sandbox, because it's sharing resources with other sandboxes.

What you can do is wrap an allocator, with a custom accounting layer, and use this to drive your decisions. I.e, here is a very trivial example:

Then we can wrap the global allocator, and see how much our cache is using:

Now, a single atomic, while is great for an example, does have some perf overhead. So, one of the crates that I have created, while keeping in mind performance, is thresher: an accounting allocator with a callback on threshold. It uses a combined "local" task/thread and "global" counter to avoid atomic contention, feeding back in every 64KiB of allocation.

thresher gets its name from the cutest shark: the Thresher Shark.

Now, what you can do with thresher is, use it to trigger callbacks when allocations are hit:

One production use case, is that we're using thresher on logfire to provide us heap profiles of our rust services when memory hits a configured threshold. I did a deep dive into heap profiles and why they are extremely useful in an older blog: a tale of two lengths. In thresher you can find a jemalloc example where you can instrument this yourself!

OK so we can control memory when it is dropped, we can use memory accounting to know how much memory we're using, what's left? How about where it goes?

This is probably the more esoteric of the 3 examples I wanted to give. There are some situations where you actually need to control where the memory lives, and sometimes by doing some allocation tricks you can get better performance out.

One example would be what smallvec and friends do. Instead of going straight to the heap to allocate things, they have a small amount that lives on the stack, and only if allocations go above a certain size, then do they write to the heap.

While smallvec is more battle tested, here is some example code about how you could do this with the allocator API:

Then we can use our toy stack first allocator:

Et voila! We have smaller allocations on the stack and then push to the heap as needed. This can give some good performance boosts.

Normally when you align memory allocations, this is based upon the thing that is being allocated for. I.e, is it a u64? align to 8 bytes or a u32? align to 4. If it's not correctly aligned, this can cause undefined behaviour and all sorts. You notice in both the bump and small stack example I had to do some shenanigans to find the next appropriately aligned address. However, there is some scenarios where the alignment of memory is external to what is being allocated.

In linux, when you read anything from disk via standard syscalls, you are usually reading from the kernel's page cache. I.e, the spare memory the kernel has around to make things transparently fast. Most of the time that is fine, but there are some times when you want to bypass it.

I.e, there is a long standing bug in kubernetes that can cause pod eviction if you are using the page cache. Or: if you are doing your own caching layer, sometimes it doesn't make sense to double up on memory devoted to caching files.

So, there is a bailout provided, in the guise of O_DIRECT that allows you to directly access files from the file system. However: one of the requirements of using this flag is that you are reading or writing into memory that is aligned to the device's logical block size. This is usually a multiple of 512, but can be less or more depending on the hardware.

The implementation of a block aligned allocator is pretty simple, here's one where we just hardset it to 4096:

With this, we can now write simple code to read directly using O_DIRECT:

Here, the read_exact call can fail on some devices if we're not using block size aligned allocations.

Like with the stack first allocation, there are libraries that allow you do this already, such as the aligned-vec crate, with their own data types to work nicely.

But here's the rub: say you had an application where you wanted to blend and mix in different allocation strategies: some vecs you want to be block aligned, some you want allocated on the stack, but you want to be able to use shared methods for both. Do we want to use smallvec and aligned-vec in order to deal with a data structure that is essentially the same thing, just allocated differently?

std allocators allows you to be generic over the collections, regardless of allocator used:

It's going to take a bit of time for the ecosystem to catch up to custom allocators. A lot of popular crates have an MSRV policy that precludes them from using even new standard features, and some existing crates, which I would think are a shoe in for the new allocator API, as of writing do not yet have support.

The libs team isn't done yet. This is the MVP of allocators, and, like I mentiond in the the last article, this is the beginning of custom allocator support. There is still work to go to support other collection types like maps etc.. so much to be done. I think that what we have is useful enough to start using it now, and also to start adapting and allowing library consumers the ability to provide their own allocators with their API.

I'm excited to see what people build, and what other use cases are unlocked with it!

#9838. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

#9837. Objections to .php application being published on ICANN site

After Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php1, ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their new gTLD program site2. They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private company effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project.

The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting":3

WordPress contributor Jamie VanRaalte objected on the grounds of "Part of a pattern - .php should not go to one company" and also said the .wordpress application was a similarly inappropriate power grab of another open-source project:4

Web developer Ryan Maietta highlighted the "File Extension Confusion and Security Risks" of using an established filetype as a TLD and the risk of people confusing websites using this domain as being officially endorsed by the PHP project:5

Forensic analyst Herbert Bärschneider also objected simply on the grounds of confusing the TLD with the filetype:6

And finally, the ICANN-affiliated Mark William Datysgeld described .php as being "Not viable from a technical perspective"7 highlighting that he has already had issues creating the page for it on the PHP-based ICANN Wiki site, causing it to return a 404 error response8:

#9836. What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia to Microsoft's recent cloud outage.

AI companies are high-value targets for nation-state actors and cyber-espionage groups, but the recent Nvidia scandal shows the threats extend beyond the cyber realm.

As discussed in a previous "What We Missed" episode, an explosive report by The New York Times last month claimed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. While Nvidia initially denied any impropriety, Huang resigned last week and admitted to extramarital affairs, with one such affair involving Alice Huang.

According to reports, US officials suspected Alice Huang to be working on behalf of China's Ministry of State Security, which had targeted Jensen Huang with a "honey trap" — a type of social engineering scheme that uses romantic relationships to manipulate individuals and gather sensitive information. The scandal, which shook the US technology industry and affected Nvidia's stock price, illustrates the severe risks — both cyber and physical — facing AI companies these days.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Also on tap: Last week's Microsoft 365 outage sparks concerns about the downstream effects of patching a growing number of vulnerabilities; and the Indian technology firm eMudhra lands in hot water again after more of its intermediate certificates are revoked.
