The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

In 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

You must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

Yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9825. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9824. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

Here, if an application is using just one thread pool for the entire journey, it has a good potential to bring the system down. We'll talk more in detail about thread pool in the coming slides. The next is database tail latency. There are situations where database is taking more time, maybe bad query, maybe you hit a wrong shard, hotspots, things like that. Observability gaps. You're logging too much of information. Then your GC or the JVM pauses. What do we do about it? In our case, we did three things, which actually helped us. The one is payload reduction. We were retaining a lot of information. Look at your maps. We had a key-value pair map, which was having user-related information. It had thousands of keys in it. We were returning this to 400-plus applications.

Not every application actually needs this. They probably need only 5 or 10 keys, but we were returning everything because that's all associated with the user. We didn't have the ability to request for a certain case. Now, once we changed that, that was helpful. Look at your response. Scan through each field one by one. Look to see if everything is making sense for the client, from the client perspective. Then, your retry discipline. Retry only if you're making idempotent calls. Here, again, you have to cap your limit and make sure you're giving thread pools separately for each of the downstream. That is what it is with thread pool guardrails.

I think now we started off with why a millisecond is important. We looked at budget. We also saw a request journey. How things could go wrong in that journey. Now it is time to look at some of the tradeoffs that are available. The first one is async fanout. We know what fanout is. Like one request turning into multiple. When we have such a fanout scenario, there are multiple options by which you can execute. One is doing things serially, the obvious way: one after the other. Or, see how much you could parallelize it in a couple of threads. Like whether you want to do two things at once. Then maybe your output needs to be fed for the other downstream calls. You take a judgment about it and do it. Then, if you're doing asynchronously, you also have options of running it in a separate background thread, or you want to drop an event.

Or let's say you make a fire and forget call. Like, what are the options that you have? What is making sense for your application at that moment? Maybe let's take an example to understand this better. If we take placing on an order as an example, when you take place order, there are a number of things which have to happen immediately, like after you hit on that place order button. One thing is you're supposed to receive your order confirmation email, the inventory has to get reduced. Your payment has to be made. You have to detect from the buyer, credit to the seller. Your metrics, you need to drop the metrics. Maybe giving this information to a couple of other downstream services which actually takes in this for the feedback and other things. Now when there are a lot of things, not all of these things have to happen serially.

When you take the item service response, where item has to call image, call seller details, call feedback and everything, again here there are a couple of things which needs to happen at the moment for sending the response back, but the couple of things need not happen synchronously. That is why we need to decide what needs to happen when, and see if you can move certain parts below the radar. When you want to do that asynchronously, making your configuration for a thread pool is very important. What is a thread pool? Let's compare it with, maybe you have a fixed number of workers in your kitchen. Let's say two workers. You have orders piling in. What happens? The two workers may not be able to do all the orders, and your orders are piling. Let's say you have very few orders, there's a very good chance that they bump onto each other.

Now, having this right configuration is very important. How could we go about it? What could help us to define what is the right configuration? This is where we need to check, what is our application doing? Is it an I/O intense work? Is it doing an I/O intense work, or is it doing a CPU intense work? Some examples could be, for CPU intense work, are you doing any algorithm processing? Are you doing image processing? Are you validating fields using your rules engine? Are you doing any encryption, decryption, or maybe tokenization? What are you actually doing? If you're doing all of these works, it is CPU intense work. Closer to your CPU cores, if you're using an 8-core system, maybe 8 threads, you should be good with this, with a normal load. Let's say if you're doing an I/O intense work, calling your REST service, calling your downstream, or waiting because you don't get the response, you have to wait.

You're looking at file. You're making a cache call, database call. All of these are I/O intense work. Since there is a waiting time involved, we need to make sure that you're adding more threads, taking this into account. A small example could be, if you are waiting for 80 milliseconds, and that particular downstream is capable of giving you a response in 20, the formula is the number of cores that you have times 1 plus 80 by 20, which nearly comes to about 40 threads. When you're having your CPU intense work, you are only at 8. If you're having an I/O intense work, you are at 40 now. Using the right number is very helpful. Your service could be doing both. Then you need to carefully check what your service is doing and make sure your limits are set based on that. This is no hard and fixed number.

It is more as a starting point where you should actually fine-tune it based on your results, based on the dashboards that you're seeing. Go back and fine-tune this. Also, there is one more important thing to understand, is, what is your incoming traffic? How much concurrent requests are you going to receive? That is also important to determine this thread count. A simple way could be from Little's Law, where, what is your latency? Latency into number of requests per second. If your latency is 50 milliseconds for your service and you are expected to get 500, then it's about 25 concurrent requests that you are seeing. This is even before the retries that you have to do, system getting abnormal, and things like that. This is just a starting number. Make sure you cap your threads at the right number. Along with the thread pool, the other thing which we need to be careful about is queuing.

Once you have set some number with your thread pool, if there are more requests, you need to make sure your queue size is also right, because that's where the next requests are going to be queued in. Now, let's say both your thread pool and your queue is full, then, what next? You need some rejection policy set up. What is your rejection policy? Have you carefully analyzed your rejection policy? Are you going to outright reject your request? Are you going to pick up any low priority work and remove that from your queue? What is that? You have to define that correctly, which will help you. Also, the other thing could be the memory, which you have to check, and things like that.

Next comes the caching. We don't expect everything to be returned by the service. You don't need to go to database to return every information through the service. There are moments that you have to leverage using cache. What type of a cache? What data do you put in your cache? What is the key that you're going to use in your cache? That's where all these engineering concepts lie. Are you going to use a single cache to look up all the information? Let's say, for the item information, do you want to add feedback into the cache? Is the review itself making sense or do you want to add the feedback score? Is adding item description making sense or do you want to add the price. What is making sense? What is the time? What is the benefit this is going to give? Of course, it's going to give you latency importance.

Because 5 milliseconds versus 30, and that's the tradeoff. Make sure you are building cache, which are multi-level, if possible. You don't want to make your cache bulky also. The payload in the cache shouldn't be bulky. You want to make sure that you are giving the right data, checking the payload size as well. Make sure it's not like more than a few KB. Using a cache is not going to solve all the problems until you have invalidation set right. If you're not invalidating your data as the data changes, if you're not making it accurate, then there is a chance that you're not showing the clients the right information. Then there is no point in using the cache. Invalidation becomes very important. How are you going to invalidate this data? There are a couple of options. If you set a fixed TTL, then till that time, the data is there and then it moves away.

Is that the practical approach that you want to take? Sometimes you want to change it when the actual data is being changed by the user. Then you want an event-based approach. You also have like version-based. Choose version-based only if you are sure about, is there a reliable plan to choose the exact version because you don't want to get into trouble of choosing what is the right version to be picked up. There is also another concept of stale-while-revalidate. This is where you know the information is stale, but it's ok to return that. You have to determine who are your clients. You don't want to have a checkout reading price from a cache. You want the most accurate information. You need to go to the DB for it. Choose what is your application doing, the responsibility of the application. How much delay is your client acceptable? That could be different between different clients.

If you're sending an email, it's fine to build something which is not really accurate, which can be eventually consistent. That is fine. Choose based on your clients as well. Then, we also have the option of using group-based, where it is best advised for derived or aggregated views. A general rule of thumb, maybe if you're experimenting it for the first time, will be start it with a TTL and then fine-tune it. Once you fine-tune it, use the event-based approach.

You know that you want to cache. You know how you can have the right data. Now you need to understand that data classification is important. You don't want to get into any of those compliance issues where you have added the wrong data, especially when you're in the financial industry. What are the data classifications available? Public data, anything which is public. When you search for an item, you get all this listing information. You get seller details, like what is the seller's name? Where is he selling this item from? These details. These are all publicly available. It's ok to cache it. What about internal data? Some of those unique IDs. You have UUID. Do you want to expose it outside? What about your item ID? Do you want to expose it outside? These are things that need to be determined. This is something that you need to work with your InfoSec team to understand what is the organization's level of classification, and how much they want to expose it, add it to a cache, and things like that.

What about confidential data, like name, address, phone number, things like this? Definitely, we need to encrypt it or tokenize it. Whatever is the best fit or recommendation from the InfoSec team. Now this is a time where we need to think, does it make sense to add it in cache? We are going to cache because we want to reduce the time. Now if you're adding a confidential data in the cache, be mindful that you need to pay for decrypting it or de-tokenizing it. Are you ready to accept that? Is your system ok to do that? Then, about classified information. Your SSN number, your passport number, all of this information, a strict no. You cannot cache this data.

Next, we'll move on to circuit breakers. Circuit breakers are very helpful. It helps you contain your problem area to a specific region. It doesn't allow the entire system to be brought down. Instead, it contains the problem in one specific area. In that way, circuit breaker is very important. If you take a mental model. What happens, let's say when a downstream fails, and you have 10 downstream calling, and one of the downstream suddenly starts failing, the queue starts to build up, your thread pool queue is also high, your backup queue is also high. Now, as per your system logic, you try to retry and you also have incoming requests. There is a complete possibility of system being down. You are actually having a self-inflicted failure. Even if there is a request which does not need this downstream A, the request could fail for them. A circuit breaker helps in that.

It helps you contain that. It is important to use this. When the circuit breaker is open, it's not going to allow any request. It's going to allow time for the particular downstream to prepare itself, to come back up. When it partially opens up to send a few requests is to see whether it succeeds. Once it succeeds, it sends the remaining requests. This is very helpful.

Then, what about fallbacks? Maybe we could take this example. When you're viewing an item on a search, you actually see this hottest item trigger, or you see this, five people are viewing onto this item. I have 10 purchased this item two hours back, or an hour back. All of these are hot information which are available. You need to be more accurate to give this information, or maybe nearly accurate. What if we don't have this? What if the service which returns this information are failing? Then you probably go and use your fallback text, which is like, maybe, yes, this is a hot item. Many people are viewing. We had more transactions. Don't give the exact number. This is the use of fallback. Consciously decide based on what your service is doing. Check if there are any places where you could use this tactic of a fallback.

It doesn't have to be a static text. It could also be defaulting to certain numbers based on the situation. The other one is data partitioning, which is mostly underrated. The main theme is to avoid hotspots. Why do we want to avoid hotspots? Because we want to distribute the traffic to all the shards possible. When you're deciding about partitions, make sure you choose a key which will give you a unique distribution across. Don't choose something like, I'm going to put all my hot sellers into one shard, like the top sellers into one shard. When there is a specific season, for example, Thanksgiving in the U.S., it's going to make all the requests go into that shard. It does not make sense to divide your sharding based on this theme. Rather use a key which is very generic: maybe the ID of the user itself, maybe his login name.

Use things which are generic, and make sure that gives a default distribution or a common distribution into all the shards. Sometimes due to regulations, it is also required that you need to split your data based on the region. Like EU region, you need to have a separate shard. U.S. region, you need to have a separate shard. This does not solve the problem because, again, if you have a seasonal event, it's going to go into that particular shard. That is why it is important to subdivide it based on the other keys that you have.

Now that we have seen a quick recap, we started with why is latency important, why is being fast important. We saw a request journey. We saw a list of tradeoffs. Now, until we measure, we don't know how good we are performing. That is why measuring things is really important. A measure could tell you how long things went well, or did not go well. Tracing will tell you why something happened. If you're not having tracing, you are missing out on something, on identifying why the problem even happened. Tracing is very important. If you haven't built it, it's time to actually build this. There could be themes, with the teams coming up saying, "My Redis is failing. My DB looks fine, but my cache calls are failing." How are we figuring out all of these things? Only because we have tracing built. You are able to take just the unique ID, look through the complete request, and see where exactly the problem has happened.

If you are able to identify, that's because you have tracing built in. Let's move on to having SLOs. Before maybe going into SLOs, I want to touch base on SLIs, service level indicators. They are like direct metric information. Let's say you are getting 100k requests per second. Then let's say around 95k requests have succeeded, and the remaining 5k were not successful. This 95% is your success rate, or your application's availability is just 95%. The same thing, you could track for your error rates, you could track for a specific error also. You have that specific downstream, you can tie it based on the feedback system, what is the availability of the feedback system. All of those things could be done. You could also have measures like, how many of my requests is responding well within 200 milliseconds? If the number was 99.8, then that is the time that you have done it.

How do we tie this to a goal? That's where SLO comes in, service level objective. Let's say you want to make sure in a 30-day period, I want the availability of my system to be 99.9. Then that is your SLO. What happens when you set this up? You are going to be alerted. The team is going to be alerted. The leaders are going to know, when an SLO, the buffer, the time that you had, if you're utilizing that buffer in a week, which you had set for a month, then it is time to pause on all your velocity works that you're doing, and first fix the system. Did I make a wrong judgment about the SLO? My SLO number itself, did I do a mistake in configuring that, or should I go back and check my application service? Check the path, where is it going wrong?

Has it been happening consistently? Then there is something to do about it. Then there is some refactoring which needs to be done. There is no one solution which can fix it. You have to do small things at every journey to make sure that you're getting it right. This is where SLO is very helpful. Thread pool observability. We saw about thread pools and the importance of thread pool. Now, if we don't have an observability dashboard, you are not going to know whether your queue is getting built up. Am I getting an alert for it? Setting up alerts, before that, you need a dashboard. We need dashboards for active threads. What is my queue size? What is a completed task count? Then, what is my rejection rate? If I have information for all of these, then it's helpful for me to fine-tune during the next iteration.

Now that we have seen about how we could measure, how we could fix it, we have seen a lot about technical things going wrong, technical aspects going wrong. Now it is time to look at the human side of things. What is within our control? What can we do as a team to get this done? That's where culture comes into picture. During planning, are we talking about SLA? Are we talking about latency? Are we talking about what is our goal? During retrospective, did we talk about the last incident which happened? What was the last issue where you had to come back online and check things on a weekend? Did you have to spend your night over it? What was that incident? Are we discussing it as a team? Are we trying to fix our dashboards? Are we trying to fix our alerts? I know that teams set up alerts only in Slack, and your Slack thread is filled up with all these alert messages, nobody is looking into it.

Are we looking into that? These are things collectively which a team needs to take up, like during your planning session, during your retrospective. This is nothing but performance and review. What are some of the anti-patterns which we need to avoid? Considering staging data. Let's say you're doing a load test in staging and taking that number for your production. That's no way the same. Your environment in your lower region is not the same as what you're doing in production. Do not take that as a benchmark. If you're going live, maybe start with 1%, 2% traffic. Or even better, start it with traffic mirroring, if that is allowed. You mirror your traffic and see whether your new flow that you've added is performing at the same level as earlier in production. Is it delaying your latency? Is there something that you need to restructure? The other things could be synchronous logging, where you're logging too much information.

What is the future holding for us? There are a lot of things, like capabilities around adaptive routing where routing could be done to regions which are having less traffic. AI-assisted predictions, you can have models to predict, this is the hot cache. Make sure you can warm it up beforehand. You can use predictive warming. Edge-native executions, all of these are in the future.

Let me give you some information which you could try before the weekend. When you go back, what could you do? Choose a simple flow in your application, from end to end. Note it down. Work with your lead. Is there any journey that could be removed? Is there any duplicate logic? I've also seen these patterns when I'm reviewing code between the teams. If there is a dependency X, and you have three flows, like A is calling B, B is calling C. You always have this X which is getting called in all the flows. You tend to have that one service which everybody wants. What do we go about it? Is there anything that you can do about changing it? These are all things that you can check. Now, instrument it, and budget. You'll note down what is the graph. If you don't have a p99 dashboard, create one.

Note down what was the current latency. If it is at 500, yes, note it down. Look at the different junctions, your paths. Note down what each path has taken up. Now, where do you want to go from here? What is your budget? Cap it. Make improvements. Remove that unnecessary call. Rephrase it. Add thread pools. Parallelize it, if it's possible. Add cache if it's not there. Do all of these things, and take a result out of it. Run an L&P and take a result out of it. Now you can check the before and after metrics. I would like to leave with one quote. We are what we repeatedly do, so excellence is not an act, but a habit. I hope we inculcate that as a habit.

Participant 1: With regards to p95 and p99, what are they? Is it percentile?

Participant 2: I have one question around serialization and that you mentioned that we should clear up if it is not required. How do we measure the cost between clearing up the data before it gets serialized and to be returned versus just sending the entire data and then hoping that it will work?

Saranya Vedagiri: This is where your logging is helpful. Let's say you're calling x downstream service and you have the log from your application level and you also have the logging from your downstream. They will tell you, I received the request at 10, I returned back at 10, 10, or whatever, that milliseconds. In your logging, you would have not got the time that they had mentioned, so look at that. There is a buffer in between. Is that adding up, between what they say as they have sent to what you have received? There can be only a certain buffer for your network. If you are seeing a 50 milliseconds difference, then there is something going wrong. Is it your queue or is it your size? There is no one direct indicator, but it could be either of these two things.

#9822. China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

During the last wave of major VMware vCenter security updates, a China-nexus threat group likely already had its next zero-day up its sleeve.

Chinese state-sponsored hackers have been using a newly disclosed VMware zero-day vulnerability and an array of custom malware to compromise victims' virtualization stacks for several months.

In October, Mandiant described a campaign by China's Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool. The group used a zero-day to breach the edge appliance, then stole credentials and secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. Exactly what that downstream compromise looked like, though, was unclear at the time.

It appears now that BeyondTrust was merely an entrée to a deeper, more interesting, and much more complex campaign. In a follow-up blog post this week, Mandiant researchers described a chained attack beginning with BeyondTrust, moving through obscure Linux appliances, and landing on VMware technologies, at which point the attackers utilized another zero-day and more than half a dozen malware programs to totally undress their targets' virtual machine (VM) environments.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

That zero-day has only now come to light, months since China first exploited it. In a security advisory, VMware owner Broadcom recommended that customers update their systems. Tracked as CVE-2026-123890, the vulnerability allows for authentication bypass in VMware vCenter and earned a "critical" 9.8 out of 10 score in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).

From tagged Remote Support boxes, Mandiant observed Armory Castle scanning a victim's internal environment, looking for open ports associated with VMware.

Instead of going for the goods immediately, the group established forward operating bases inside other, possibly unrelated Linux appliances in the same network. These appliances lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) visibility, allowing the group to establish persistence and stage its malware arsenal away from the parts of the network where defenders were looking. Among other malware, it was there that Armory Castle deployed "Bonesaw," a Go-based remote exploitation tool customized for vCenter.

The VMware vCenter Server is the central control plane used to manage multiple VMs and their ESXi hosts. Because it oversees everything else, few technologies are more useful for lateral movement, ransomware attacks, etc., than vCenter is. It's why this summer, the disclosure of two critical vCenter vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310, caused a stir.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

While organizations were rushing to patch the two vCenter vulnerabilities known to Broadcom, Armory Castle appears to have had an extra one up its sleeve. In September, it was able to use Bonesaw against a victim that had already patched its vCenter; Bonesaw was tuned to exploit CVE-2026-123890, a flaw that stems from the vCenter login system's use of predictable, time-based UUIDv1 timestamp generation in Secure Remote Password (SRP) authentication handling.

Exploiting CVE-2026-123890 afforded Armory Castle a shared session key it could use to create new authenticated sessions as an administrator, bypassing the normal authentication process entirely. Bonesaw then paid more dividends, automating the process of copying vCenter's internal directory database and creating powerful new accounts for further damage.

At this point, Armory Castle had total control over the victim's vCenter. Yet it continued on with machine-like focus; the attackers deployed a tool called "Sawsnake" to turn the Bonesaw-stolen vCenter login-signing key into forged authentication tokens, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) and enabling impersonation of any user. It then jumped to ESXi hypervisors and found and extracted system files.

For high-risk organizations, updating VMware instances to patched versions can't be the end of the story.

Related:AI Agents Zip From Flaw Discovery to Root Access in 11 Minutes

Because vCenter is just so sensitive, Mandiant urged organizations not to rely solely on patching known vulnerabilities as they come up. It pointed to its vSphere Defender's Guide, published earlier this spring. Its recommendations include the standard fare — promptly updating and isolating management systems, encrypting particularly sensitive systems, and applying especially tight controls to administrator accounts — but also offers more pointed items. It notes that vCenter doesn't necessarily record all important operating system (OS) activity, and that sophisticated attackers can delete local logs post-compromise; therefore, organizations should consider forwarding logs to a separate security information and event management (SIEM) platform.

Mandiant researchers also advised that organizations not rely on vCenter's built-in firewall, as it has too many limitations. For example, it doesn't generate remote logs for rejected connection attempts or certain shell activity, doesn't enforce policies for data egress, and, most of all, it's simply at risk for being built into the very system it's designed to secure.

"Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities," the researchers wrote.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9821. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

#9820. How Security Vendors Are Tackling Access-Control Challenges for AI Agents

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Identity, runtime, and development controls are converging as enterprises look for ways to keep agents within their assigned jobs. But vendors' approaches vary, so CISOs face a choice.

As organizations expand their use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to perform tasks traditionally done by employees, security teams must control not only which systems agents can access but which actions they are authorized to take.

The Blueprint Alliance, an industry group advocating for coordinated controls, notes that 92% of organizations use autonomous AI agents, but only 34% secure them with the same rigor as they do for human users.

Many vendors have begun adding capabilities to better control agents. Their approaches overlap, leaving CISOs to determine how the new offerings fit into a coherent security architecture that keeps agents focused on their assigned tasks and prevents overpermissioning machine identities beyond what their human users can access.

Earlier this month, CrowdStrike introduced what it calls an AI Kill Switch, which gives security teams a way to block an agent's access to AI models via connected gateways. The AI Kill Switch, launched during CrowdStrike's Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona, extends Falcon Guardian, the AI detection and response offering that supports Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints. Guardian discovers agents and controls which ones may run and connects prompts, identities, tool calls, and skills to downstream actions in an execution graph.

Related:Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

The kill switch works with CrowdStrike's Falcon AI Gateway or connected third-party gateways. Its current enforcement point is model access, rather than every system an agent can reach. CrowdStrike says it will later extend the capability to terminate agent processes and revoke their access to enterprise resources.

"The hardest case is the agent that behaves abnormally without breaking a business process rule," CrowdStrike's chief product officer AJ Shipley said during an Oct. 29 media roundtable discussion.

Discussing agent insider threat detection, Shipley described an approach that establishes a baseline of expected agent and user behavior and then detects deviations, even when no explicit policy violation occurs.

CrowdStrike also announced earlier this month agreements to acquire two startups — Fiddler AI and Dreadnode — extending its push into agent observability and predeployment security testing. Fiddler evaluates agents and helps explain their behavior in production, while Dreadnode tests models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment. The Wall Street Journal reported a combined purchase price of approximately $495 million. The acquisitions have not yet closed.

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

CrowdStrike is one of several vendors addressing agent access controls. Anaconda is combining agentic software development with autonomous security testing, Cisco and Teleport are tying access to infrastructure identity, Okta is enforcing identity policy when agents call tools, and Fortinet is extending controls over execution and application behavior.

Anaconda, for instance, is approaching the problem through application development by pairing agentic software development with autonomous security testing. Last month, it expanded its AI Dev Factory, combining development agent swarms with autonomous red-team agents that probe models, agents, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for weaknesses. The release incorporates technology from Anaconda's August acquisition of Enkrypt AI, supporting red teaming across more than 300 attack categories and runtime guardrails that approve, modify, or block risky behavior.

Anaconda's earlier acquisitions of Outerbounds, Kilo Code, and Enkrypt AI collectively bring together production orchestration, agentic development, and AI security.

"Our road map out for all three acquisitions would have been about two or three years’ worth of engineering effort," Anaconda CEO David DeSanto says, describing Enkrypt as the final component needed to accomplish this goal.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

Testing agents is one requirement; limiting their authority in production is another. Cisco is approaching that problem through infrastructure identity, becoming Teleport's largest strategic investor in August. Teleport's open source platform replaces passwords and permanent SSH keys with ephemeral certificates.

Teleport CEO Ev Kontsevoy describes an incident in which a customer deployed an agent to process data and update a database. When the intended database became unavailable, the agent found another and tried to update it. The agent was trying to complete its assignment rather than respond to an attacker. Its improvisation nevertheless exposed the difference between granting access and containing behavior.

"Would you say it's a security accident or what? Whatever it is, it's terrifying when it happens, particularly at scale," Kontsevoy tells Dark Reading.

Cisco and Teleport's partnership addresses containment through verified infrastructure identities and access granted "just in time, just enough," says Peter Bailey, Cisco's senior VP and general manager for security.

"We want to be able to take action and stop action based upon identity," Bailey says.

On Oct. 26, Cisco introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, applying the partnership's infrastructure-identity approach to administrators and agents. Cisco says it provides temporary, identity-bound access to network infrastructure, records sessions, and ends privileges when the task is complete.

Kontsevoy describes attaching privileges to tasks rather than permanently assigning them to accounts. A deployment ticket could identify the engineer, laptop, and CI/CD pipeline involved. Each is granted necessary privileges, which disappear when the ticket closes. Teleport's MCP gateway also enforces policy and tracks relationships among initiating actors, agents, and subagents, he says.

When an agent acts on an employee's behalf, controls must distinguish the agent's permissions from those of the person directing the agent to avoid inappropriate privilege escalation.

Consider a scenario in which an HR assistant runs on a service account that can read every employee record. A contractor asking the agent for the CEO's compensation could get the response since the assistant has access the contractor doesn't. According to Okta, this agent would be a "confused deputy," as it exercises authority the requester lacks.

To address this scenario, Okta's Agent Gateway treats agents as "first-class" identities; it preserves the distinction between their permissions and those of the users directing them. It requires a credential that identifies both the user and the agent and uses token exchange to preserve the delegation context. The gateway limits the tools available, while the downstream MCP server enforces the user's record-level access. Agent Gateway is now generally available as an addition to AI agents, an identity-security offering made generally available in April.

In an Oct. 8 blog post, Okta described plans for Cross App Access support and a gateway-based kill switch. Officials said the latter "will make agent deactivation immediate, down to tokens already issued, by rejecting any request carrying a token issued to a deactivated agent."

Okta is not alone in extending identity controls to agents. At its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September, CrowdStrike announced Agentic Identity Provider, designed to establish trusted agent identities, broker time-limited access, and link actions to initiating employees or systems.

Microsoft is pursuing a related approach through Project Perception, connecting agent identity, behavioral risk signals, and access controls across its security products via its new Guardian Agent capabilities.

Meanwhile, Fortinet is extending AI inspection across its existing network security products. Last month, the company announced the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service for FortiGate customers and described expanded FortiAIGate capabilities incorporating Virtue AI technology, which Fortinet acquired earlier this year. Virtue AI adds policy-derived guardrails, continuous assessment, code analysis, and agent red teaming.

Fortinet executive vice president Anthony James describes more than 50 simulated application environments in which customers can test agent boundaries before connecting to real systems. He says Virtue can block an agent from communicating with MCP tools or servers not approved for its task and detect prompt sequences that progress from innocuous to malicious.

FortiAIGate began by monitoring communications to and from AI infrastructure, James adds. Customers deploying agents sought a deeper understanding of the application. Models, MCP servers, agents, and skills "require a little deeper application knowledge than just interpreting the network traffic," he says.

Overlapping approaches have prompted coordination efforts. In September, Okta announced the Blueprint Alliance with vendors including AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler. The group aims to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors' products.

The alliance has outlined principles for agent identity, task-scoped access, monitoring, and containment. Whether those principles translate into interoperable products and expanded adoption remains to be seen.

Taken together, these approaches point to a common requirement: keeping an agent's access tied to its assigned task. Identity verification, security testing, and runtime monitoring address different parts of that requirement, but no single control confirms that an agent will remain within its assignment.

Emerging control planes aim to connect those controls across tools and systems — limiting agents to their assigned tasks rather than letting AI software determine how far its authority extends.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. Earlier contributions include Pro Sound News, Television Broadcast, Videography, Sound & Communications, Post magazine and Crain’s Electronic Media. Jeff holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Communications and Journalism from Adelphi University. More details are available on Jeff’s LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeffaschwartz.
