#9780. Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 23: Cyber insurers share their view of the AI-driven threat landscape and how mounting challenges are putting pressure on both sides of the policy, leaving the current model unsustainable.

Cyber insurance providers are approaching 2027 facing a fundamental challenge. Claims rose 40% in 2024 and another 20% in 2025, even as premiums have stayed largely flat. This trend is something both Coalition and Travelers say isn't sustainable; and at the center of that shift is AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape not by inventing new attack types, but by making existing ones — ransomware, business email compromise, and phishing — dramatically easier to execute at scale.

In this episode of Dark Reading Confidential, Dark Reading media and projects director Becky Bracken and Dark Reading senior news director Rob Wright sit down with Lauren Winchester, vice president of cyber-risk services at Travelers; and Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition, to unpack what the data actually shows. The conversation moves past the headline-grabbing surge in disclosed vulnerabilities to a more nuanced picture: exploitation is rising, but not as sharply as disclosure volume, while AI-powered phishing kits are bring sold SaaS-style to criminals with little technical skill, driving a measurable spike in BEC and ransomware activity.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The two insurers also agree on where the real exposure lies: not necessarily with large enterprises, which have the resources to track threat intelligence and patch quickly, but with small and mid-sized businesses that often lack an in-house IT team altogether. That awareness gap, they argue, is where insurers now have to step in — not just to underwrite risk, but to actively help policyholders defend their organizations against it.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please listen to the podcast or watch the video.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, where we bring you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. My name is Becky Bracken. I'm an editor with Dark Reading, and I am thrilled today to do just that: deliver as promised, along with my colleague Rob Wright. Today we are going to be talking about all things cyber insurance and AI. In addition to my very smart colleague Rob Wright, who I mentioned, we are thrilled to welcome Lauren Winchester, who is vice president of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance, and of course Daniel Woods, who is the head of emerging risk at Coalition. Welcome to both of you. Thank you.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

DR's Becky Bracken: This conversation got started actually in one of our editorial meetings, and Rob had the smartest take, and then won the dubious distinction of getting to lead the conversation, which is always a problem around here when you have a smart idea. So, I am going to get out of the way and let Rob explain some of his very smart thinking around this topic, and get you guys in on it.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: It wasn't a smart idea, but it was a question about what is happening with cyber insurance now that we have all this AI stuff going on. Thank you for joining me on this. We'll start with a basic question about where the cyber insurance industry is right now today in 2026, going into 2027. Just broad strokes. I know it's still somewhat of a new market, but where do you feel like it is in terms of overall health and growth? Daniel, why don't you kick us off?

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So I think the best data source on the state of the market comes from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, who publish an annual report about the US market, and that shows this paradoxical situation where the number of policies being issued are growing, but the number or the amount of premium being collected is pretty much stable.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

We also see claims are increasing; they rose 40% in 2024, 20% in 2025. So I think the cyber-insurance market is beginning to ask whether prices are sustainable, especially given some of the changes we'll discuss today related to AI.

DR's Rob Wright: And Lauren, what's your take on what the industry is today?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think we're at a period of uncertainty right now, as most industries are. AI is likely to change a lot of the ways that we work, a lot of the ways that threat actors engage with companies and attack companies, and ultimately that uncertainty is something the industry is grappling with.

DR's Rob Wright: So I know I'm a bit of a pessimist among my Dark Reading colleagues. I try not to be pessimistic, but obviously AI has had a huge effect on the cybersecurity landscape this year. Ever since Project Glasswing, Mythos, and the tsunami of reported vulnerabilities, disclosed vulnerabilities, increases in zero-days. That's really put a lot of companies, a lot of vendors, and enterprises on the defensive. So, what effect is that having?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important not to conflate the surge in vulnerabilities being disclosed with a surge in attacks that drive cyber claims, at least not just yet. As many of your listeners will know, not all vulnerabilities are created equal, and so certainly there are thousands more vulnerabilities being disclosed in the months since Mythos preview came out, as compared to earlier in the year, and that's going to have an impact. If we want to look at what's a good stand-in for exploitation, you can look at CISA's known exploited vulnerability list. There's a little lag there, but ultimately, if you look at the KEVs, you can see an increase that's happening, but it's not to the same order of magnitude as the overall CVE and vulnerability disclosure. But certainly, there is an increase. I think we just looked at this recently through Sept. 30, and CISA had added 246 KEVs in 2026, which exceeded the 245 added in total for 2025 when we looked at it. So naturally, we are on a trend to exceed last year.

We think maybe it'll be about a third more than last year, when we get to the end of the year, not a trend you want to see, but it's not in the same almost-exponential curve you're seeing with the total vulnerabilities. And I don't mean to be like everything's fine, right?

We also put out a report yesterday, and we look at ransomware leak site data as well as potential indicators of activity, and that's where ransomware threat actors are posting on their Dark Web leak sites who their victims are, and ultimately for Q3 2026, that activity was up. So certainly, the activity with the financially motivated threat actors is picking up, and we've also seen that in our business email compromises (BECs) as well, so it's painting a picture of more activity for sure. But just good to note that increased volumes don't necessarily mean increased tax immediately.

DR's Rob Wright: Gotcha. And I'll just say you are allowed to be positive on this podcast. Coalition's Daniel Woods: So to bring a bit of gloom, I'd say the conversation also needs to look beyond just vulnerabilities and exploits. AI is a general-purpose technology, and it impacts not just the exploitation of vulnerabilities, but other mechanisms.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: And it's that experimentation that's happening right now. #9779. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9776. It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Bot detection has become a losing game. Security teams need to limit privileged access for humans and their machine counterparts equally.

The Internet is flooded with bots. People use them to organize their emails, shop, chat, and handle some of their busywork.

At the other end of the spectrum sit attackers who want to increase their speed just as much as, if not more than, legitimate users. The faster they can conduct distributed denial-of-service attacks or brute-force password attacks, the quicker they can breach an organization and the more victims they can claim.

The line between legitimate and illegitimate activity grows finer by the minute, as bots have become pros at mirroring human behavior — even its flaws. For example, during the infamous incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, bots reportedly found ways to communicate with one another by accessing the outside Internet — something they weren't programmed to do.

Behavioral baselines that security teams once relied on are becoming moot, since bots can impersonate humans. As the volume of bots accelerates, the real question isn't human versus bot but what that activity is telling teams and how to police it.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Security tools will miss something, so teams should choose systems that allow them to quickly edit, adjust, and continually adapt to a changing environment, explains Jeremy London, director of engineering, AI, and threat analytics at Keeper Security.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents, which can perform automated actions similar to bots without human oversight, are only adding to environmental complexities. While some advancements can be exciting, they also introduce more gaps and zero-day vulnerabilities to the attack surface that "we just didn't understand," London says.

"I think the continual effort, as a security organization, is to show up with the right tooling, understand what you're trying to solve for, and then be able to react quickly because your control plane probably missed something — that's a guarantee," London tells Dark Reading.

Organizations underwent significant transformations over the past decade, propelled by AI. Adoption moved at a scale that "no one ever predicted," London says. That has forced teams to cut corners on important safeguards.

Code reviews and security practices need a serious makeover, especially regarding boundaries and compliance. Bots and agents have new levels of autonomy and access, leading to more unpredictability and changing what security risks even look like.

However, such a makeover has proved to be a difficult undertaking because AI doesn't come with a security playbook, London explains. A decade ago, bots were rigid and scripts performed a single action. Now "teams vibe code stuff and throw things at the wall and see what works, and the scale that [bots] can operate at is totally different," he says.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

While organizations struggle, attackers are having a field day with these advancements. Given all of the recent disclosures and reports, it's no surprise that attacks are rising. What is surprising is how quickly threat actors can adapt and respond to countermeasures, says Jérôme Segura, VP of threat research at DataDome, a bot management and agent trust platform.

"Anytime we put challenges in front of them, we see it slows them down and costs them more because to run the same operation, they have to use more resources, which becomes expensive," he explains.

The reason the attackers aren't giving up despite the obstacles is that their attacks are working, Segura tells Dark Reading.

"Because the payout is so great, they're doubling, tripling their investments," he says.

The persistence is challenging and frustrating for defenders. But it's just the stark reality that threat actors are highly motivated, and "we're battling against that," Segura adds.

When threat actors use bots against online retailers, they replicate the exact flow of a human but without all the telltale signs, such as hesitating over a purchasing decision, fumbling to enter card or shipping details, or pausing to solve a CAPTCHA challenge. They don't need to click through every page like a human would or wait for the site to load all the images either. As a result, bots complete transactions in a split second, Segura says. The speed can create security risks and unfair competition for legitimate users.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

More concerningly, bots complete these tasks in ways that appear legitimate because they're aware that companies are trying to block this malicious activity, he says. And the volume is only increasing. Segura conducted research analyzing traffic hitting retailers' product pages and found that 91% were actually bad bots.

Taking legal action is difficult when it's nearly impossible to differentiate legitimate and illegitimate activity, which puts even more pressure on businesses. Scraping product pages or ticket scalping remains "kind of a gray area in terms of the legal aspect," Segura explains, adding that the law isn't quite clear yet on what is permitted.

In some cases, the culprits are organized groups just looking to make money and oftentimes use loopholes to circumvent the law. For example, they end up using existing infrastructure to collect scarce products and resell them, Segura says.

Threat actors organize so that they have specialties, just as defenders do, he has observed. Some specialize in reverse engineering specific parts of a website's code to understand how it works. Others focus on providing the necessary infrastructure, including all the IP addresses, to carry out those kinds of attacks, he says.

"You can source IPs from real users that are extremely convincing because they're also shared by humans," Segura explains. "So all these specializations within these groups, working well together, and making sure everybody's getting paid, is really interesting."

Behavioral analytics are struggling right now, London says, and is a "pain point" rippling across the industry.

Some bots can move the mouse pointer and send keystrokes to mimic typing, so verification techniques like measuring mouse movements or typing speeds need to evolve. Models can be a bit slow, just as humans can be, he notes.

"Although they are robotic in nature, some of those behavioral or human factors that teams have been using for indication points are really close," London says.

Since it's so difficult to determine whether activity is from a human or a bot, organizations should manage them both the same way when it comes to privileged identity: the less access, the better.

Given all of the risks and potential blast radii, "security teams, not developers, should probably decide whether AI is allowed in an organization," London recommends.

"From a security perspective, it makes it somewhat simple because AI agents can do bad things [and] humans can do bad things," he says. "So if we just look at it through that perspective, I don't care if it's a human or an agent."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9775. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

InfoQ Homepage News Meta Brings Code Review Auto-Approval More Mainstream with PyTorch GreenLight

Nov 27, 2026 4 min read

GreenLight has started letting a PyTorch AI reviewer approve pull requests from its own maintainers. It is an open-source take on RADAR, the system Meta uses to land low-risk code changes without waiting on a human. The move comes as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and Sonar all describe ways to automate approval itself.

RADAR stands for Risk Aware Diff Auto Review. Meta described it in a paper published in May. The paper starts from a capacity problem. Significant lines of code per human-landed diff rose 105.9% year over year, and diffs per developer per month rose 51%.

Meta attributes more than 80% of that increase to agentic AI assistance. Review has not kept pace, and the share of diffs reviewed within 24 hours is dropping. The authors describe their response in narrow terms.

Rather than attempting to replace code review broadly, RADAR targets automation to diffs that satisfy conservative safety criteria.

RADAR sorts each diff by author and source before anything else. Deterministic codemods can be approved through a blanket policy and skip per-diff AI review. AI-generated codemods and automated runbooks go through a pipeline of safety checks, a Diff Risk Score and an LLM reviewer. Any failure sends the diff to a human.

RADAR pipeline for AI and bot diffs. Source: Meta, "Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta" (arXiv 2605.30208)

The safety checks are hard limits. Open-source code, SOX-scoped code and code that needs extra review are never eligible. Runbooks must show a clean 60-day record, with zero production incidents and low revert and rejection rates. They are also capped at up to 2,000 diffs per day.

The Diff Risk Score works as a percentile gate. Allowlisted runbooks can land diffs up to the 50th percentile of risk. Other AI and bot sources stop at the 20th. Human-authored diffs default to the 5th, and each organization can tune its own thresholds.

The last gate is the RADAR Review Agent, which reads the actual change. It looks for safe patterns such as dead code removal, refactoring without behavior change, logging additions and new tests. The paper sets a strict bar for the agent.

For a diff to be auto-accepted, ACR requires a confidence score of at least 8 out of 10, with all changes classified into safe categories.

Approved bot diffs do not land at once. They wait in a landing queue for a configurable delay, shown as 24 hours in the paper's pipeline diagram. A human can still reject a diff during that window. Meta also monitors the funnel and tunes thresholds over time.

PyTorch said in May that it would rebuild RADAR in the open. In a PyTorch devlog, Edward Yang wrote that "the RADAR approves are good" in Meta's internal use. He also set the rule that shapes GreenLight today.

RADAR is predicated on trust of the author, so RADAR approves will be limited to PyTorch maintainers who otherwise already have approval rights on the files being changed.

GreenLight follows that rule. Its cohort comes from the people listed in PyTorch's merge rules. A PR only gets a real verdict when a merge rule names its author. Everyone else is reviewed in shadow mode, and those reviews never become approvals.

A scan runs every five minutes and sends eligible PRs to a reviewer workflow. A land verdict approves the PR and labels it. A no-land verdict withdraws any earlier GreenLight approval. The README adds that "a reverted PR is dropped from every path, permanently."

OpenAI described a similar policy at QCon San Francisco 2026. Brian Yang, member of technical staff at OpenAI, said a few engineers began building ChatGPT Ads with Codex in November 2025, and the codebase has zero human-written production code.

Yang matches approval to the change. Everyday changes are auto-approved once required checks pass. Critical changes must pass sandbox validation against a copy of production traffic, and then a human decides. His target is at least 90% auto-approval for routine PRs.

The team tunes its automated reviewer every week. Engineers read past approvals, blocks and missed breakages, then test new thresholds against history. When too many bad PRs open, they fix the agent. When bad PRs keep merging, they fix the checker. Anthropic applies the same idea to the actions an agent takes while it works with its Antique code review system.

Sonar frames approval as part of what it calls the agentic software factory. Manish Kapur, VP of product marketing and developer relations at Sonar, wrote that in a well-run factory "the factory knows which changes can pass on automated evidence and which require a person to decide." Sonar's latest developer survey shows the pressure behind that. Of more than 1,000 respondents, 76% said they generate AI code faster than they can verify it, and only 39% always check it before committing.

The common thread is scoped trust. Meta and PyTorch gate approval on author trust and a calibrated risk score. OpenAI gates it on the type of change, and Anthropic on what an action could break. In each case, reverts and misses feed back into the system.

Developers interested in learning more can read the RADAR paper here and find GreenLight's source here.

#9772. Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

Researchers discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages as part of a fake recruitment campaign that spreads malware and gives attackers access to developers' machines.

A coordinated supply chain campaign is targeting .NET developers with fake coding assignments, weaponized software dependencies, and GitHub-hosted malware capable of stealing browser credentials and establishing remote access.

Researchers at Socket discovered the campaign, which involves 13 malicious NuGet packages designed to compromise Windows-based developer environments through seemingly legitimate job assessments, according to a report published this week. The packages use fake job "Home Assessment" projects to target Windows .NET developers, with most posing as button controls for WinUI 3 and WPF, which are user interface frameworks for building applications.

"In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable," Socket researcher Kush Pandya wrote in the report.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

As in similar campaigns that weaponize developer repositories and code packages, attackers are exploiting developers' willingness to download, build, and run code they believe to be trustworthy. In this case, the malicious code is disguised as part of job-recruitment exercises for .NET developers. Such campaigns can turn routine development activities into infection vectors, potentially spreading malware and malicious code through the software supply chain.

NuGet is a package manager for .NET. Socket researchers traced the campaign across NuGet, GitHub repositories, and malicious code embedded in development projects, identifying packages linked through shared attack infrastructure and techniques.

The most recent example they found was a GitHub repository created on Nov. 4 that contained a purported WinUI 3 assessment called "Mini File Vault & Tracker." The project instructed candidates to complete a three- to four-hour development exercise using a supplied Visual Studio project. However, its dependencies contained malicious code.

"Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026," Pandya wrote in the report.

Socket could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reached candidates, as researchers found "no recruiter message, email or job post for them," he added.

The attack involved two malicious NuGet packages working together. One executed code after every project build, while the other launched a staged executable when the application created its button control. This effectively turned an ordinary development workflow into an infection chain.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

The investigation eventually uncovered 13 unique package names and 28 versions across those packages, as well as four NuGet publisher accounts linked to the operation.

Characterizing the campaign as posing a very serious threat to enterprises, Pandya says attackers could gain access to a "treasure trove" of sensitive information by compromising a developer's machine.

"A developer's machine holds source code, SSH keys, GitHub, package registry and cloud tokens, and browser sessions that have often already passed multifactor authentication," Pandya tells Dark Reading. "In this campaign, building the take-home project was enough to run the threat actor's code."

Beyond access to terminals and configuration files, many developers who work from a console have their command history automatically collected, he says. This can give adversaries insight into the commands developers have executed, as well as access to passwords and API keys that may have been inadvertently pasted into the command line, he adds.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Moreover, by disguising their activity as legitimate development work, attackers gain a degree of stealth and control once the malicious code is running on a developer's machine, he says.

"A threat actor could extract SSH keys and network configurations, but their access is still from an external host and must go through various security controls," Pandya explains. "If they are working directly from a developer's machine, they not only have the necessary access keys but also the expected IP address and geolocation to avoid suspicion."

As adversaries continue to weaponize code packages from legitimate sources to compromise the software supply chain, developers and security teams must remain vigilant. Socket has recommendations for both.

Developers should treat take-home coding assignments and unfamiliar projects as untrusted code, Pandya advises. Before building them, they should check for unfamiliar NuGet dependencies, additional package sources, and build scripts that could execute automatically.

"Open take-home tests and unfamiliar repositories only in a disposable virtual machine with no credentials," he recommends. "Restrict which package sources projects can use, scan dependencies before they are installed, and verify recruiters through official channels."

Organizations should also restrict which NuGet feeds developers can use and review third-party packages that contain build scripts capable of executing commands, according to Socket. They should also educate employees and job candidates about fake recruitment assessments to reduce the risk of attackers exploiting the hiring process to gain access to developer environments.

Security teams, meanwhile, should identify affected developer machines and treat suspected infections as potential credential and software supply chain compromises, rather than simply malware incidents, Pandya says.

"If a machine is compromised, isolate and reimage it, rotate credentials and tokens from a clean device, revoke active sessions, and review audit logs," he says.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

The Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The following table shows how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

#9769. Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

A previously undocumented Iranian threat group called "Volant Manticore" is targeting Cypriot organizations as part of an intelligence-gathering effort for Tehran.

Cyprus' growing security ties with Israel and its use as a staging ground for Western forces operating across the Middle East appear to be making the island an increasingly attractive target for Iranian cyber espionage.

Volant Manticore is an early example of that interest. The previously undocumented advanced persistent threat (APT) group has been targeting organizations in Cyprus as part of what researchers at Check Point describe as an Iranian intelligence-gathering campaign focused on the island.

Its targets so far have included a Cyprus-based airline operating primarily between Cyprus and Israel, telecommunications providers, critical infrastructure organizations, and a suspected government entity with military connections. The selection of targets suggests an effort to gather intelligence on the island's government, infrastructure, and relationships with regional partners, the researchers said.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

Check Point has assessed with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is likely an offshoot of the Iranian threat group MuddyWater, tasked primarily with spying on Cypriot organizations on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is among the first known Iranian groups to have a dedicated focus on Cyprus, although it has recently expanded its targeting to organizations in Saudi Arabia, says Sergey Shykevich, director of threat intelligence at Check Point Software.

"Cyprus' defense and energy ties with Israel and Greece, along with its role in Western military operations in the region, may help explain why it is a target for intelligence gathering," Shykevich says.

He points to a Check Point report from earlier this year on a surge in attempts by Iran-linked actors to exploit vulnerabilities in Internet-connected surveillance cameras across the Middle East, including Cyprus, beginning on Feb. 28, when US and Israeli strikes against Iran began. Access to the cameras could have provided Iranian intelligence with a way to monitor military and other strategically important facilities, gather information ahead of potential attacks, and assess the damage from strikes afterward. "The timing is another indication of how Iranian cyber activity tracks with security developments in the region," Shykevich adds.

Check Point described Volant Manticore as relying heavily on phishing to gain an initial foothold using lures tailored for the organizations and sectors it targets. The security vendor's investigation of the group began when it spotted a fabricated resume on VirusTotal associated with "Athena Marinou," a fictitious, AI-generated travel-and-tourism professional.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

The document directed recipients to download the full CV from what appeared to be a legitimate recruitment website. The link, however, pointed to an archive hosted on Catbox, which delivered KuboShell — a custom backdoor that the group is using to establish an initial foothold on compromised systems, conduct basic reconnaissance, and receive commands from its operators.

Check Point found that the Windows-based backdoor uses the decentralized InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communications, potentially making them harder to block or disrupt than communications routed through a conventional attacker-controlled server. The malware allows attackers to collect details about compromised systems and networks using basic PowerShell instructions. Check Point found evidence that the group then deployed a more extensive, multistage post-compromise toolkit it calls the Homa Framework.

Volant Manticore also uses legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software such as N-able, NetLock, and MeshCentral in its campaigns. The tools enable remote access and administrative capabilities while allowing the attacks to blend in with legitimate traffic. Check Point also identified infrastructure associated with credential-harvesting campaigns, including domains designed to resemble corporate email services. The researchers found evidence of operators testing their malware against antivirus products and using virtual machines and VPN-related software in their operational environments.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Check Point's analysis showed overlaps between Volant Manticore's techniques and code and those used by the long-active Iranian group MuddyWater. However, Check Point assessed Volant Manticore is a separate operation likely run by former MuddyWater members. "The group has a well-developed toolkit that combines techniques we’ve seen from MuddyWater with tools it developed itself," Shykevich says. "One of the less common techniques we observed was its use of KuboShell, a backdoor that provides remote access and communicates through IPFS, a decentralized file-sharing network."

In September, Check Point observed the group suddenly broadening its focus to include Saudi Arabia. "We are currently seeing the group active in both countries," Shykevich says. While Cyprus remains its primary espionage target, the group has been targeting Saudi organizations as well, mainly in the healthcare sector, he adds. "The increase in activity coincided with escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The scale of the group's activity in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere is likely to vary as the situation in the region evolves."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9768. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.
